record.title: HM Revenue & Customs reports about £4.6 billion of additional tax yield in 2024–25 from cases flagged by its Connect data-matching system
record.summary: HM Revenue & Customs estimates that cases flagged by its Connect data-matching system yielded about £4.6 billion of additional tax in 2024–25.
record.account: HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) launched Connect in 2010–11. In its annual report, HMRC calls Connect an information technology system that joins a billion pieces of data across its tax regimes to help identify fraud. In February 2015 the National Audit Office called Connect a good illustration of HMRC's ability to use new technology. It cited HMRC's figures. About £80 million had been invested since 2008. Extra revenue was £3 billion. Drawing on HMRC's annual report, it said that Connect let HMRC cut its Risk and Intelligence staff by 40% while it collected more compliance revenue. In the report in HMRC's 2024–25 accounts, the Comptroller and Auditor General records that HMRC used TRUCE (Transaction Risking Upstream in a Connect Environment). It served to stop repayments of value-added tax that may require investigation, once it had identified them. It did the same for repayments of income tax. A system called IDRS replaced it from August 2023. Officials describe Connect's methods as data analytics with risk rules. None of them calls Connect AI. Pinsent Masons reported on 8 October 2025 a freedom-of-information response from HMRC. In it, HMRC said that Connect cases generated an average £3.4 billion of additional annual yield, about £4.6 billion in 2024–25. Around 4,300 staff use the system. The Comptroller and Auditor General notes that compliance yield is HMRC's own estimate of the revenue that it considers it generated. The estimate includes the losses that it prevented. That is the measure behind the £4.6 billion. In its annual report for 2025–26, ordered printed on 9 July 2026, HMRC credits AI and advanced analytics with the protection and recovery of £10 billion in tax in 2025–26. It does not name Connect.

HMRC reports about £4.6 billion of extra yield from Connect cases in 2024–25. In a case study of 2015, the National Audit Office draws on HMRC's own annual report. It says that Connect let HMRC cut its Risk and Intelligence staff by 40% while it collected more compliance revenue. Both are measurable gains in HMRC's results. The figures are HMRC's own estimates, and the Comptroller and Auditor General describes compliance yield as such.
The tax office has not traced the extra revenue to an effect on the public, such as funded services or a smaller tax gap.

fields.summary: HM Revenue & Customs estimates that cases flagged by its Connect data-matching system yielded about £4.6 billion of additional tax in 2024–25.
fields.account: HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) launched Connect in 2010–11. In its annual report, HMRC calls Connect an information technology system that joins a billion pieces of data across its tax regimes to help identify fraud. In February 2015 the National Audit Office called Connect a good illustration of HMRC's ability to use new technology. It cited HMRC's figures. About £80 million had been invested since 2008. Extra revenue was £3 billion. Drawing on HMRC's annual report, it said that Connect let HMRC cut its Risk and Intelligence staff by 40% while it collected more compliance revenue. In the report in HMRC's 2024–25 accounts, the Comptroller and Auditor General records that HMRC used TRUCE (Transaction Risking Upstream in a Connect Environment). It served to stop repayments of value-added tax that may require investigation, once it had identified them. It did the same for repayments of income tax. A system called IDRS replaced it from August 2023. Officials describe Connect's methods as data analytics with risk rules. None of them calls Connect AI. Pinsent Masons reported on 8 October 2025 a freedom-of-information response from HMRC. In it, HMRC said that Connect cases generated an average £3.4 billion of additional annual yield, about £4.6 billion in 2024–25. Around 4,300 staff use the system. The Comptroller and Auditor General notes that compliance yield is HMRC's own estimate of the revenue that it considers it generated. The estimate includes the losses that it prevented. That is the measure behind the £4.6 billion. In its annual report for 2025–26, ordered printed on 9 July 2026, HMRC credits AI and advanced analytics with the protection and recovery of £10 billion in tax in 2025–26. It does not name Connect.

record.title: Cheshire Police facial recognition matches CCTV to an 18-year-old county lines dealer, who gets 28 months while a second dealer gets 34
record.summary: Cheshire Constabulary's facial recognition system matched CCTV of an unknown Northwich dealer to an 18-year-old. Police stopped him with a 19-year-old on 17 May 2024. Both were jailed on 1 July 2024.
record.account: In its release, Cheshire Constabulary states that in April 2024 officers in Northwich learned of a phone number used by the “Kyle” county lines gang. They recovered closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage of an unknown man suspected of using it. The force's facial recognition system matched the image to an 18-year-old from Connah's Quay. On Friday 17 May 2024 officers on patrol spotted the 18-year-old on Winnington Street with a 19-year-old. A search of the 18-year-old found 99 wraps of crack cocaine worth about £990. It found a hunting-style knife. The 19-year-old had two phones. He had a lock knife. He had £960. Both pleaded guilty. On 1 July 2024 Chester Crown Court jailed the 18-year-old for 28 months and the 19-year-old for 34 months. Police Constable Dean Butterworth said that the 18-year-old was not known locally. He said that the footage helped officers identify him quickly as a suspect. He said that facial recognition helped. The BBC's Local Democracy Reporting Service reported on 10 February 2026 that there were 973 positive identifications using facial recognition across Cheshire in 2025. Cheshire Police described this as a 60% rise on the year before. The Police and Crime Commissioner said that the technology has been used retrospectively in Cheshire and is not used in real time.

record.title: France's tax administration reports that its Foncier innovant tool found 140,000 taxable swimming pools in 2023, but one section of its report gives more than 120,000
record.summary: Foncier innovant, a tool of France's tax administration, found 140,000 taxable pools in 2023 in aerial photographs. The administration values them at €40 million in local tax.
record.account: In October 2021 the Direction générale des Finances publiques (DGFiP), France's tax administration, introduced Foncier innovant, an algorithmic tool. The tool detects pools on IGN aerial photographs. It detects buildings the same way. It compares them with declarations. An agent then checks each detection. In 2022 the DGFiP found 20,000 pools in an experiment in nine départements (20 Minutes, 12 June 2024). On 2 June 2023 the DGFiP announced that Foncier innovant would cover all of metropolitan France in 2023. From the end of May 2023 it wrote to more than 120,000 owners of detected pools, asking them to regularize their declarations. On 20 March 2024 Thomas Cazenave, minister for public accounts, presented the first assessment of the government's anti-fraud plan at Bercy. Cazenave said that the tool had detected 140,000 undeclared swimming pools, which would let local authorities collect about €40 million in property tax. Owners received DGFiP letters asking them to regularize their declarations (RMC, Ouest-France, 21 March 2024). In Ouest-France on 21 March 2024, Olivier Vilois of the CGT Finances publiques union cited colleagues in the field. By their account, the algorithms' error rate stood at 55 to 60% at the time. On 24 March 2024 ici (France Bleu) reported on the Dordogne public-finance office. It had found about 1,500 undeclared pools in 2023 among some 30,000 in the département. The office would send notices to catch up on property tax by the end of March. CNews (11 June 2024) cites the DGFiP annual activity report as reported by Ouest-France. CNews gives 140,000 pools identified in 2023, with €40 million that should have been paid in 2023. In the section on pool controls of its 2023 annual report, the DGFiP gives 140,000 taxable pools in 2023, against 20,000 in 2022. It puts the additional local property tax at €40 million. In a separate overview of the cadastre, the DGFiP gives more than 120,000 pools. It does not explain the difference. No result for individual communes has been published. In October 2024 the Cour des comptes reported that Foncier innovant raised the number of taxed pools in the nine pilot départements by 5.7% (20,356 pools). The Cour reported that in 2022 the tool brought in €4.4 million in recurring revenue, with €5.7 million in back-tax. The Cour added that the €40 million for 2023 is a DGFiP estimate. It found that the tool produces many false positives that agents must clear. In April 2026 the DGFiP extended the campaign to verandas along with garages. The goal was €100 million (France 2).

evidence.quote_translation: The public finance office of Dordogne spotted some 1,500 swimming pools not declared to the tax authorities in Dordogne during 2023, out of the department's roughly 30,000 swimming pools.

fields.account: In October 2021 the Direction générale des Finances publiques (DGFiP), France's tax administration, introduced Foncier innovant, an algorithmic tool. The tool detects pools on IGN aerial photographs. It detects buildings the same way. It compares them with declarations. An agent then checks each detection. In 2022 the DGFiP found 20,000 pools in an experiment in nine départements (20 Minutes, 12 June 2024). On 2 June 2023 the DGFiP announced that Foncier innovant would cover all of metropolitan France in 2023. From the end of May 2023 it wrote to more than 120,000 owners of detected pools, asking them to regularize their declarations. On 20 March 2024 Thomas Cazenave, minister for public accounts, presented the first assessment of the government's anti-fraud plan at Bercy. Cazenave said that the tool had detected 140,000 undeclared swimming pools, which would let local authorities collect about €40 million in property tax. Owners received DGFiP letters asking them to regularize their declarations (RMC, Ouest-France, 21 March 2024). In Ouest-France on 21 March 2024, Olivier Vilois of the CGT Finances publiques union cited colleagues in the field. By their account, the algorithms' error rate stood at 55 to 60% at the time. On 24 March 2024 ici (France Bleu) reported on the Dordogne public-finance office. It had found about 1,500 undeclared pools in 2023 among some 30,000 in the département. The office would send notices to catch up on property tax by the end of March. CNews (11 June 2024) cites the DGFiP annual activity report as reported by Ouest-France. CNews gives 140,000 pools identified in 2023, with €40 million that should have been paid in 2023. In the section on pool controls of its 2023 annual report, the DGFiP gives 140,000 taxable pools in 2023, against 20,000 in 2022. It puts the additional local property tax at €40 million. In a separate overview of the cadastre, the DGFiP gives more than 120,000 pools. It does not explain the difference. No result for individual communes has been published. In October 2024 the Cour des comptes reported that Foncier innovant raised the number of taxed pools in the nine pilot départements by 5.7% (20,356 pools). The Cour reported that in 2022 the tool brought in €4.4 million in recurring revenue, with €5.7 million in back-tax. The Cour added that the €40 million for 2023 is a DGFiP estimate. It found that the tool produces many false positives that agents must clear. In April 2026 the DGFiP extended the campaign to verandas along with garages. The goal was €100 million (France 2).

fields.summary: Foncier innovant, a tool of France's tax administration, found 140,000 taxable pools in 2023 in aerial photographs. The administration values them at €40 million in local tax.
fields.account: In October 2021 the Direction générale des Finances publiques (DGFiP), France's tax administration, introduced Foncier innovant, an algorithmic tool. The tool detects pools on IGN aerial photographs. It detects buildings the same way. It compares them with declarations. An agent then checks each detection. In 2022 the DGFiP found 20,000 pools in an experiment in nine départements (20 Minutes, 12 June 2024). On 2 June 2023 the DGFiP announced that Foncier innovant would cover all of metropolitan France in 2023. From the end of May 2023 it wrote to more than 120,000 owners of detected pools, asking them to regularize their declarations. On 20 March 2024 Thomas Cazenave, minister for public accounts, presented the first assessment of the government's anti-fraud plan at Bercy. Cazenave said that the tool had detected 140,000 undeclared swimming pools, which would let local authorities collect about €40 million in property tax. Owners received DGFiP letters asking them to regularize their declarations (RMC, Ouest-France, 21 March 2024). In Ouest-France on 21 March 2024, Olivier Vilois of the CGT Finances publiques union cited colleagues in the field. By their account, the algorithms' error rate stood at 55 to 60% at the time. On 24 March 2024 ici (France Bleu) reported on the Dordogne public-finance office. It had found about 1,500 undeclared pools in 2023 among some 30,000 in the département. The office would send notices to catch up on property tax by the end of March. CNews (11 June 2024) cites the DGFiP annual activity report as reported by Ouest-France. CNews gives 140,000 pools identified in 2023, with €40 million that should have been paid in 2023. In the section on pool controls of its 2023 annual report, the DGFiP gives 140,000 taxable pools in 2023, against 20,000 in 2022. It puts the additional local property tax at €40 million. In a separate overview of the cadastre, the DGFiP gives more than 120,000 pools. It does not explain the difference. No result for individual communes has been published. In October 2024 the Cour des comptes reported that Foncier innovant raised the number of taxed pools in the nine pilot départements by 5.7% (20,356 pools). The Cour reported that in 2022 the tool brought in €4.4 million in recurring revenue, with €5.7 million in back-tax. The Cour added that the €40 million for 2023 is a DGFiP estimate. It found that the tool produces many false positives that agents must clear. In April 2026 the DGFiP extended the campaign to verandas along with garages. The goal was €100 million (France 2).

details.value: U.S. Customs and Border Protection uses the system to check arriving travelers against passport or visa photos that the government holds, to catch impostors and speed entry.

details.label: Contribution of the AI
details.value: The facial comparison (less than two seconds, according to CBP) produced the mismatch that triggered secondary inspection. The search and removal were human actions. The documentation is CBP's own release, as the deployer, and an NBC report with a named CBP official. The vendor of the algorithm and the match threshold are not known. record.summary: On 22 August 2018 CBP's new facial comparison system at Dulles flagged a mismatch for a man presenting a French passport. Officers found a Congolese ID in his shoe. He was returned to Brazil.
record.account: On 22 August 2018, the third day of facial comparison biometrics at Washington Dulles International Airport, a 26-year-old man arrived from Sao Paulo. He presented a French passport at primary inspection. In a release, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) states that the officer used the facial comparison technology. It confirmed that the man did not match the passport. In secondary inspection officers found his authentic Republic of Congo identification card concealed in his shoe. CBP Area Port Director Daniel Mattina told NBC News that the man was apprehended. He said that officers processed him. He said that they returned him to Brazil. CBP called him the first impostor detected with the technology. The vendor of the matching algorithm has not been named. In a September 2020 audit, the U.S. Government Accountability Office reported that CBP officials said that air entry facial recognition had helped identify seven impostors by December 2019. Gizmodo reported on 11 February 2021 that, in its annual report for fiscal year 2020, CBP showed no impostor flagged at any airport that year. CBP had scanned over 23 million travelers at entry, exit and Preclearance points. Gizmodo also reported that CBP facial recognition detected fewer than 100 impostors at pedestrian crossings that year. In a release of 24 September 2021, CBP reports that facial biometrics had stopped, by September 2021, more than 900 impostors nationally since September 2018.

fields.summary: On 22 August 2018 CBP's new facial comparison system at Dulles flagged a mismatch for a man presenting a French passport. Officers found a Congolese ID in his shoe. He was returned to Brazil.
fields.account: On 22 August 2018, the third day of facial comparison biometrics at Washington Dulles International Airport, a 26-year-old man arrived from Sao Paulo. He presented a French passport at primary inspection. In a release, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) states that the officer used the facial comparison technology. It confirmed that the man did not match the passport. In secondary inspection officers found his authentic Republic of Congo identification card concealed in his shoe. CBP Area Port Director Daniel Mattina told NBC News that the man was apprehended. He said that officers processed him. He said that they returned him to Brazil. CBP called him the first impostor detected with the technology. The vendor of the matching algorithm has not been named. In a September 2020 audit, the U.S. Government Accountability Office reported that CBP officials said that air entry facial recognition had helped identify seven impostors by December 2019. Gizmodo reported on 11 February 2021 that, in its annual report for fiscal year 2020, CBP showed no impostor flagged at any airport that year. CBP had scanned over 23 million travelers at entry, exit and Preclearance points. Gizmodo also reported that CBP facial recognition detected fewer than 100 impostors at pedestrian crossings that year. In a release of 24 September 2021, CBP reports that facial biometrics had stopped, by September 2021, more than 900 impostors nationally since September 2018.

record.title: Pindrop's deepfake detector traces a fake Biden robocall in New Hampshire to ElevenLabs. A Berkeley team agrees. The FCC cites the finding
record.summary: Pindrop ran its deepfake audio analysis against more than 120 voice engines. It traced a fake Biden robocall before New Hampshire's January 2024 primary to ElevenLabs. The FCC later cited it.
record.account: Voters in New Hampshire received an AI-generated robocall impersonating President Biden before the 23 January 2024 primary. On 25 January 2024 Pindrop, a company that builds synthetic-audio detection tools, published its analysis of a 39-second clip on its website. Pindrop checked the clip's patterns against more than 120 voice synthesis engines. Its chief executive, Vijay Balasubramaniyan, told WIRED that the result came back well north of 99 percent for ElevenLabs. Hany Farid's team at the University of California, Berkeley, was initially skeptical. It ran its own model on the same sample. The team concluded with high confidence that the audio was AI-generated and likely made with ElevenLabs. ElevenLabs' own detector returned 84 percent, a result that WIRED reproduced. New Hampshire Public Radio reported on 23 May 2024 that the New Hampshire Attorney General had announced 26 charges against Steven Kramer. It reported that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had proposed a $6 million fine. The sources do not show that the state charges drew on Pindrop's analysis. On 24 May 2024 the FCC stated in its proposed fine against Kramer that the robocall had been made with software from a website run by Eleven Labs. For that statement it cites Pindrop's analysis and an NBC News report. A New Hampshire jury acquitted Kramer of the state charges on 13 June 2025. Kramer told the Associated Press that he would not pay the FCC's fine.

fields.summary: Pindrop ran its deepfake audio analysis against more than 120 voice engines. It traced a fake Biden robocall before New Hampshire's January 2024 primary to ElevenLabs. The FCC later cited it.
fields.account: Voters in New Hampshire received an AI-generated robocall impersonating President Biden before the 23 January 2024 primary. On 25 January 2024 Pindrop, a company that builds synthetic-audio detection tools, published its analysis of a 39-second clip on its website. Pindrop checked the clip's patterns against more than 120 voice synthesis engines. Its chief executive, Vijay Balasubramaniyan, told WIRED that the result came back well north of 99 percent for ElevenLabs. Hany Farid's team at the University of California, Berkeley, was initially skeptical. It ran its own model on the same sample. The team concluded with high confidence that the audio was AI-generated and likely made with ElevenLabs. ElevenLabs' own detector returned 84 percent, a result that WIRED reproduced. New Hampshire Public Radio reported on 23 May 2024 that the New Hampshire Attorney General had announced 26 charges against Steven Kramer. It reported that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had proposed a $6 million fine. The sources do not show that the state charges drew on Pindrop's analysis. On 24 May 2024 the FCC stated in its proposed fine against Kramer that the robocall had been made with software from a website run by Eleven Labs. For that statement it cites Pindrop's analysis and an NBC News report. A New Hampshire jury acquitted Kramer of the state charges on 13 June 2025. Kramer told the Associated Press that he would not pay the FCC's fine.

record.title: Medicare's Fraud Prevention System helps catch $654.8 million in inappropriate payments in 2015
record.summary: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services count $654.8 million in inappropriate Medicare payments identified or prevented in 2015 with help from their Fraud Prevention System.
record.account: The report “Fraud Prevention System Return on Investment, Fourth Implementation Year” of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) is undated. The Wayback Machine archived it on 24 August 2016. In it, CMS states that the Fraud Prevention System (FPS) helped identify or prevent $654.8 million in inappropriate payments during calendar year 2015, about 44% more than the previous year. That total counts actions taken due to the FPS. It counts investigations that the system expedited. It counts those that it augmented. It counts those that it corroborated. CMS gives a corrected return on investment of $11.5 to $1. The originally reported $11.6 contained a rounding error. In Table 1, identified savings are $115.4 million in the first year (July 2011 to June 2012). They are $250.1 million in the second. They are $454.0 million in the third. The cumulative total is $1,474.3 million. The savings come from claims denied by pre-payment edits. They come from payment suspensions. They come from projected cost avoidance after billing privileges were revoked. They come from overpayments referred for recovery. The value of referrals to law enforcement was $49.2 million in 2015. CMS says that the Office of Inspector General of the Department of Health and Human Services certified the methodology. It counts 45 providers on active payment suspension at year end. Costs were an estimated $57.1 million. They include $19.5 million for a developing contractor. They include $4.8 million for a modeling contractor. CMS does not describe the system's technique. In a report of 30 August 2017, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that FPS leads started about 20 percent of contractor fraud investigations in fiscal 2015 and 2016. GAO found that these investigations led to corrective actions. It found that they led to savings. Contractor officials told GAO that FPS generally did not speed up investigations once they began. GAO notes that CMS estimated actual savings of $133 million for 2014 against $454 million identified. CMS reported to GAO that FPS edits denied nearly 169,000 claims in fiscal 2015. It reported that they saved $11.3 million. In fiscal 2016 the edits denied nearly 324,000 claims. They saved $20.4 million. CMS had 24 prepayment edits in place by May 2017.

fields.account: The report “Fraud Prevention System Return on Investment, Fourth Implementation Year” of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) is undated. The Wayback Machine archived it on 24 August 2016. In it, CMS states that the Fraud Prevention System (FPS) helped identify or prevent $654.8 million in inappropriate payments during calendar year 2015, about 44% more than the previous year. That total counts actions taken due to the FPS. It counts investigations that the system expedited. It counts those that it augmented. It counts those that it corroborated. CMS gives a corrected return on investment of $11.5 to $1. The originally reported $11.6 contained a rounding error. In Table 1, identified savings are $115.4 million in the first year (July 2011 to June 2012). They are $250.1 million in the second. They are $454.0 million in the third. The cumulative total is $1,474.3 million. The savings come from claims denied by pre-payment edits. They come from payment suspensions. They come from projected cost avoidance after billing privileges were revoked. They come from overpayments referred for recovery. The value of referrals to law enforcement was $49.2 million in 2015. CMS says that the Office of Inspector General of the Department of Health and Human Services certified the methodology. It counts 45 providers on active payment suspension at year end. Costs were an estimated $57.1 million. They include $19.5 million for a developing contractor. They include $4.8 million for a modeling contractor. CMS does not describe the system's technique. In a report of 30 August 2017, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that FPS leads started about 20 percent of contractor fraud investigations in fiscal 2015 and 2016. GAO found that these investigations led to corrective actions. It found that they led to savings. Contractor officials told GAO that FPS generally did not speed up investigations once they began. GAO notes that CMS estimated actual savings of $133 million for 2014 against $454 million identified. CMS reported to GAO that FPS edits denied nearly 169,000 claims in fiscal 2015. It reported that they saved $11.3 million. In fiscal 2016 the edits denied nearly 324,000 claims. They saved $20.4 million. CMS had 24 prepayment edits in place by May 2017.

value.text: Identified savings rose each year, from $115.4 million in the first implementation year to $654.8 million in 2015. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services reported to the Government Accountability Office that the edits denied nearly 169,000 claims in fiscal 2015 and nearly 324,000 in fiscal 2016. The agency had 24 prepayment edits in place by May 2017.

record.title: NHC's 2025 season verification: Google DeepMind ensemble mean outperformed official short-range Atlantic track forecasts in NHC's first operational use of AI models
record.summary: In 2025, its first season with AI models in operations, the US National Hurricane Center found that Google DeepMind's ensemble mean beat its official Atlantic track forecasts at 12 to 72 hours.
record.account: James Franklin, a former branch chief at the US National Hurricane Center (NHC), shared his own verification of the 2025 season in late October 2025. Michael Lowry relayed it on 3 November 2025. CNN reported it on 3 December 2025. Franklin found that the DeepMind ensemble was the most accurate guidance on track in the 2025 season. He found that it was the most accurate on intensity. CNN added that it did not perform evenly with each storm. NHC dated its Forecast Verification Report for the 2025 season 30 March 2026. In it, NHC states that 2025 marked the first time that NHC incorporated AI-based models into real-time operations. In the Atlantic track comparison, the Google DeepMind ensemble mean (GDMI) slightly outperformed the official forecast at lead times from 12 to 72 hours. Official forecasts outperformed the consensus aids TVCA, HCCA and FSSE. In the eastern North Pacific, GDMI performed much better than every other individual model. It beat the official forecast at 48 to 120 hours. At those lead times it beat all consensus aids. For intensity it was the top individual model from 12 to 48 hours. GDMI was not available early in the season, so the first storms are excluded from these comparisons. On 10 September 2026 Lowry reported that Franklin's numbers showed DeepMind ahead of NHC's official track forecasts for a second year.

In its verification, NHC measured lower Atlantic track errors for the DeepMind ensemble than for its official forecast at 12 to 72 hours. An independent analysis found that the ensemble was the most accurate guidance of the season. NHC gained a measurably better tool in operations.
The sources measure the accuracy of forecasts. They do not measure a change in public warnings, actions or losses across the season that the AI caused.

data.retained_case_account: The National Hurricane Center's Forecast Verification Report for the 2025 season is dated 30 March 2026. It states that 2025 marked the first time NHC incorporated AI-based models into real-time operations. In the Atlantic track comparison, the Google DeepMind ensemble mean (GDMI) slightly outperformed the official forecast at lead times from 12 to 72 h. Official forecasts outperformed the consensus aids TVCA, HCCA and FSSE. In the eastern North Pacific, GDMI performed considerably better than every other individual model. It beat the official forecast and all consensus aids at 48–120 h. For intensity it was the top individual model from 12 to 48 h. GDMI was not available early in the season, so the first storms are excluded from these comparisons.

fields.account: James Franklin, a former branch chief at the US National Hurricane Center (NHC), shared his own verification of the 2025 season in late October 2025. Michael Lowry relayed it on 3 November 2025. CNN reported it on 3 December 2025. Franklin found that the DeepMind ensemble was the most accurate guidance on track in the 2025 season. He found that it was the most accurate on intensity. CNN added that it did not perform evenly with each storm. NHC dated its Forecast Verification Report for the 2025 season 30 March 2026. In it, NHC states that 2025 marked the first time that NHC incorporated AI-based models into real-time operations. In the Atlantic track comparison, the Google DeepMind ensemble mean (GDMI) slightly outperformed the official forecast at lead times from 12 to 72 hours. Official forecasts outperformed the consensus aids TVCA, HCCA and FSSE. In the eastern North Pacific, GDMI performed much better than every other individual model. It beat the official forecast at 48 to 120 hours. At those lead times it beat all consensus aids. For intensity it was the top individual model from 12 to 48 hours. GDMI was not available early in the season, so the first storms are excluded from these comparisons. On 10 September 2026 Lowry reported that Franklin's numbers showed DeepMind ahead of NHC's official track forecasts for a second year.

fields.account: James Franklin, a former branch chief at the US National Hurricane Center (NHC), shared his own verification of the 2025 season in late October 2025. Michael Lowry relayed it on 3 November 2025. CNN reported it on 3 December 2025. Franklin found that the DeepMind ensemble was the most accurate guidance on track in the 2025 season. He found that it was the most accurate on intensity. CNN added that it did not perform evenly with each storm. NHC dated its Forecast Verification Report for the 2025 season 30 March 2026. In it, NHC states that 2025 marked the first time that NHC incorporated AI-based models into real-time operations. In the Atlantic track comparison, the Google DeepMind ensemble mean (GDMI) slightly outperformed the official forecast at lead times from 12 to 72 hours. Official forecasts outperformed the consensus aids TVCA, HCCA and FSSE. In the eastern North Pacific, GDMI performed much better than every other individual model. It beat the official forecast at 48 to 120 hours. At those lead times it beat all consensus aids. For intensity it was the top individual model from 12 to 48 hours. GDMI was not available early in the season, so the first storms are excluded from these comparisons. On 10 September 2026 Lowry reported that Franklin's numbers showed DeepMind ahead of NHC's official track forecasts for a second year.

record.account: On 25 February 2025 the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) began producing operational forecasts with AIFS Single. AIFS Single is the deterministic version of its Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System. ECMWF runs it alongside its physics-based Integrated Forecasting System (IFS). ECMWF claimed gains of up to 20% in the tracks of tropical cyclones. Pan and colleagues found that the errors of AIFS in precipitation over China were lower than those of the IFS from April 2024 to March 2025. They found that AIFS underestimated extremes. On 1 July 2025 ECMWF launched the ensemble version, AIFS-ENS, operationally. The Science Operations Officer of the National Hurricane Center said that ECMWF's AI-driven global system was available for evaluation at the center during the 2025 season. ECMWF published its evaluation of the forecasts of 2025 on 8 May 2026. It reports that AIFS errors were 5 to 15% lower than those of the IFS for most variables at the surface. The same held for most variables in the upper air. Errors in cyclone positions were much smaller, while cyclone intensity was under-predicted. No specific event in which AIFS beat the IFS is documented in the cited ECMWF sources. On its Severe Event Catalogue page for Storm Eowyn, ECMWF states that wind gusts were not available for AIFS. In July 2026 a preprint partly written by ECMWF authors restated that machine-learning forecast models “tend to dramatically underestimate intensity” of tropical cyclones. The authors proposed a correction. Zhang and Ma found that the operational AIFS had a temperature error about 15.7% lower than the IFS control forecast in Inner Mongolia in summer 2026. The IFS control forecast did better for heavy rain. So Chinese meteorologists with no ties to ECMWF confirm part of its claim in two studies.

fields.account: On 25 February 2025 the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) began producing operational forecasts with AIFS Single. AIFS Single is the deterministic version of its Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System. ECMWF runs it alongside its physics-based Integrated Forecasting System (IFS). ECMWF claimed gains of up to 20% in the tracks of tropical cyclones. Pan and colleagues found that the errors of AIFS in precipitation over China were lower than those of the IFS from April 2024 to March 2025. They found that AIFS underestimated extremes. On 1 July 2025 ECMWF launched the ensemble version, AIFS-ENS, operationally. The Science Operations Officer of the National Hurricane Center said that ECMWF's AI-driven global system was available for evaluation at the center during the 2025 season. ECMWF published its evaluation of the forecasts of 2025 on 8 May 2026. It reports that AIFS errors were 5 to 15% lower than those of the IFS for most variables at the surface. The same held for most variables in the upper air. Errors in cyclone positions were much smaller, while cyclone intensity was under-predicted. No specific event in which AIFS beat the IFS is documented in the cited ECMWF sources. On its Severe Event Catalogue page for Storm Eowyn, ECMWF states that wind gusts were not available for AIFS. In July 2026 a preprint partly written by ECMWF authors restated that machine-learning forecast models “tend to dramatically underestimate intensity” of tropical cyclones. The authors proposed a correction. Zhang and Ma found that the operational AIFS had a temperature error about 15.7% lower than the IFS control forecast in Inner Mongolia in summer 2026. The IFS control forecast did better for heavy rain. So Chinese meteorologists with no ties to ECMWF confirm part of its claim in two studies.

ECMWF reports errors 5 to 15% lower than the IFS for most variables in 2025. Researchers in Inner Mongolia with no tie to ECMWF found a temperature error about 15.7% lower in summer 2026. That is a measured improvement in forecasting, with weaker results for heavy rain, extremes and cyclone intensity.
Only the skill of the forecasts has been reported. The sources do not show an outcome for the public, such as a warning that worked better because of AIFS.

record.title: A machine learning model that flags risky Universal Credit advance requests saved the UK benefits department an estimated £4.4 million from 2022–23 to 2024–25
record.summary: A machine-learning model at the Department for Work and Pensions flags risky Universal Credit advance requests for caseworkers. The department estimates that it saved £4.4 million in three years.
record.account: Since May 2022 the Department for Work & Pensions (DWP) has used a machine learning model. The model marks potentially fraudulent claims for Universal Credit advances. It scores new claims. It refers those above a threshold to a caseworker. DWP staff make the decisions. On 6 December 2024 the Guardian reported documents released under the Freedom of Information Act. They show a statistically significant disparity in the model's February 2024 fairness analysis. It appears by age. It appears by disability. It appears by marital status. It appears by nationality. The National Audit Office (NAO) published “Tackling benefit overpayments due to fraud and error” on 22 October 2025. It reports that DWP estimates that the model saved £4.4 million from 2022–23 to 2024–25. DWP cannot separate the model's costs from wider spending on data analytics. The NAO reports DWP's finding that the model is around three times more effective at identifying fraud risk than a randomized control group sample. It reports a median payment delay of one day for referred requests. It reports DWP's fairness analysis of July 2025 for 2024–25. Older claimants (age groups 45 to 54 and above) were over-referred for review. Non-UK nationals were over-referred. Fairness analysis was possible on only one of nine protected characteristics. Four further models were in development. On the same day Civil Service World (Jim Dunton) reported the NAO's warnings on data infrastructure. It quoted Transformation Minister Andrew Western, who said that “our one machine learning model has made us significantly more effective”. On 16 April 2026 Civil Service World reported a letter from DWP's permanent secretary to the Public Accounts Committee. The model had directly saved less than £5 million in three years by marking about 7,000 requests that staff rejected. Civil Service World reported that the department admits that the model needs retraining. On 9 July 2026 DWP published an effectiveness assessment for April 2025 to March 2026. DWP reported that the live model was 2.5 times more effective at identifying high-risk advances than a random control group, and that the retrained model had not yet been deployed. It concluded that the model should keep operating.

ratings.reason: The National Audit Office reports the department's finding that the model is about three times better at identifying fraud risk than a random control sample. That is a measured gain in capability. The saving of £4.4 million over three years is small. Civil Service World reports that it rests on about 7,000 rejected requests out of more than a million advances a year.

The department has reported no outcome for claimants or the public beyond its estimated saving. Referred claimants face added evidence demands. The department's fairness analyses showed that older claimants and claimants who are not UK nationals were over-referred.

data.retained_case_account: The National Audit Office (NAO) published “Tackling benefit overpayments due to fraud and error” on 22 October 2025. It states that since May 2022 the Department for Work & Pensions (DWP) has used a machine learning model. The model flags potentially fraudulent claims for Universal Credit advances. DWP estimates it saved £4.4 million from 2022–23 to 2024–25. The model scores new claims and refers those above a threshold to a caseworker. Decisions are made by DWP staff. DWP cannot disaggregate the model's costs from wider spending on data analytics. The NAO reports DWP's finding that the model is around three times more effective at identifying fraud risk than a randomized control group sample. It reports a median payment delay of one day for referred requests. DWP's July 2025 fairness analysis for 2024–25 showed older claimants (age groups 45 to 54 and above) and non-UK nationals over-referred for review. Fairness analysis was possible on only one of nine protected characteristics. Four further models were in development. Civil Service World (Jim Dunton, 22 October 2025) reported the NAO's warnings on data infrastructure. It quoted Transformation Minister Andrew Western saying that the one machine learning model has made the department significantly more effective.

fields.account: Since May 2022 the Department for Work & Pensions (DWP) has used a machine learning model. The model marks potentially fraudulent claims for Universal Credit advances. It scores new claims. It refers those above a threshold to a caseworker. DWP staff make the decisions. On 6 December 2024 the Guardian reported documents released under the Freedom of Information Act. They show a statistically significant disparity in the model's February 2024 fairness analysis. It appears by age. It appears by disability. It appears by marital status. It appears by nationality. The National Audit Office (NAO) published “Tackling benefit overpayments due to fraud and error” on 22 October 2025. It reports that DWP estimates that the model saved £4.4 million from 2022–23 to 2024–25. DWP cannot separate the model's costs from wider spending on data analytics. The NAO reports DWP's finding that the model is around three times more effective at identifying fraud risk than a randomized control group sample. It reports a median payment delay of one day for referred requests. It reports DWP's fairness analysis of July 2025 for 2024–25. Older claimants (age groups 45 to 54 and above) were over-referred for review. Non-UK nationals were over-referred. Fairness analysis was possible on only one of nine protected characteristics. Four further models were in development. On the same day Civil Service World (Jim Dunton) reported the NAO's warnings on data infrastructure. It quoted Transformation Minister Andrew Western, who said that “our one machine learning model has made us significantly more effective”. On 16 April 2026 Civil Service World reported a letter from DWP's permanent secretary to the Public Accounts Committee. The model had directly saved less than £5 million in three years by marking about 7,000 requests that staff rejected. Civil Service World reported that the department admits that the model needs retraining. On 9 July 2026 DWP published an effectiveness assessment for April 2025 to March 2026. It concluded that the model should keep operating.

fields.summary: A machine-learning model at the Department for Work and Pensions flags risky Universal Credit advance requests for caseworkers. The department estimates that it saved £4.4 million in three years.
fields.account: Since May 2022 the Department for Work & Pensions (DWP) has used a machine learning model. The model marks potentially fraudulent claims for Universal Credit advances. It scores new claims. It refers those above a threshold to a caseworker. DWP staff make the decisions. On 6 December 2024 the Guardian reported documents released under the Freedom of Information Act. They show a statistically significant disparity in the model's February 2024 fairness analysis. It appears by age. It appears by disability. It appears by marital status. It appears by nationality. The National Audit Office (NAO) published “Tackling benefit overpayments due to fraud and error” on 22 October 2025. It reports that DWP estimates that the model saved £4.4 million from 2022–23 to 2024–25. DWP cannot separate the model's costs from wider spending on data analytics. The NAO reports DWP's finding that the model is around three times more effective at identifying fraud risk than a randomized control group sample. It reports a median payment delay of one day for referred requests. It reports DWP's fairness analysis of July 2025 for 2024–25. Older claimants (age groups 45 to 54 and above) were over-referred for review. Non-UK nationals were over-referred. Fairness analysis was possible on only one of nine protected characteristics. Four further models were in development. On the same day Civil Service World (Jim Dunton) reported the NAO's warnings on data infrastructure. It quoted Transformation Minister Andrew Western, who said that “our one machine learning model has made us significantly more effective”. On 16 April 2026 Civil Service World reported a letter from DWP's permanent secretary to the Public Accounts Committee. The model had directly saved less than £5 million in three years by marking about 7,000 requests that staff rejected. Civil Service World reported that the department admits that the model needs retraining. On 9 July 2026 DWP published an effectiveness assessment for April 2025 to March 2026. DWP reported that the live model was 2.5 times more effective at identifying high-risk advances than a random control group, and that the retrained model had not yet been deployed. It concluded that the model should keep operating.

record.title: Cases flagged by three Udbetaling Danmark fraud-control models end with benefits cut 135, 36 and 72 times in 2023
record.summary: Three of Udbetaling Danmark's machine-learning fraud models flagged cases that ended with benefits cut 135, 36 and 72 times in 2023. Amnesty International questions whether they work.
record.account: Udbetaling Danmark (UDK) is the Danish public authority that has centralized welfare payments since 2012. ATP (Arbejdsmarkedets Tillaegspension) administers its benefits. ATP designs the fraud-control components of UDK's Joint Data Unit (Den Faelles Dataenhed), which was established in 2014, according to the University of Copenhagen's Offentlig AI database. NNIT A/S is the supplier. The database lists the methods run on linked register data: profiling, machine learning, Naive Bayes classification and cluster analysis. Earlier yields come from other sources. In July 2019 the Danish legal think tank Justitia used UDK figures on its data-based controls. They led to 705 cases in 2017. In 2018 they led to 1,094. Each of these cases ended with benefits stopped, changed or repaid. Its author argues that this yield is poor for data matching that can cover up to 2.7 million recipients. The authors of the Denmark chapter of Automating Society 2020 cite the July 2019 report. They give the same counts out of 2.7 million screened beneficiaries. AlgorithmWatch (2020) reports that controls in 2017 and 2018 uncovered about half a billion kroner in erroneous payments. As of 2019 UDK was reported to use up to 60 algorithms for purposes that included fraud detection. In a letter to Amnesty International before November 2024, UDK supplied its 2023 statistics for three data-driven controls. The 2023 figures carry no day. The “Really Single” model produced 412 requested cases, 292 established control cases and 135 cases with revenue (benefits stopped or reduced). “Model Abroad” (unreported departures, state and disability pension) gave 511, 351 and 36. The parental-leave controls including the “Fictitious Employment” model gave 491, 207 and 72. UDK cautioned that cases with revenue in a year are not necessarily a proportion of cases established that year. On 11 January 2024 a control official of UDK and ATP told Amnesty that the team manages 5,000 to 6,000 cases a year, of which around 1,800 come from the models. In its report of 12 November 2024, Amnesty concludes that it is questionable whether the algorithms are effective. It finds that most opened cases end with no further action. It finds that the system risks discrimination. It finds a risk of mass surveillance. A control official of Copenhagen Municipality said that more often than not there is no fraud in the cases that UDK sends. Amnesty reports that the Danish Data Protection Authority told it that the authority acts only on two grounds. One is an inquiry. The other is a complaint. No finding by a regulator on the models is on record.

ratings.reason: No individual beneficiary of the controls is identified. The people directly affected are those investigated. By Amnesty's reading of UDK's figures, 54% to almost 90% of opened cases per model ended with no further action.

By UDK's own 2023 figures, three models produced 135, 36 and 72 cases with revenue from 412, 511 and 491 requested cases. No amounts are given, and UDK says that yearly figures are not directly comparable.

No societal outcome is reported beyond the cases with revenue that UDK counts for itself. The 2023 figures come without amounts, so the extent of any gain to public funds cannot be established, and Amnesty questions whether the models are effective.

data.retained_case_account: Udbetaling Danmark (UDK), the Danish public authority that has centralized welfare payments since 2012, has its benefits administered by ATP (Arbejdsmarkedets Tillaegspension). ATP designs the fraud-control components of UDK's Joint Data Unit (Den Faelles Dataenhed, established 2014 per the University of Copenhagen's Offentlig AI database). NNIT A/S is the supplier. As of 2019 UDK was reported to use up to 60 algorithms for fraud detection and other purposes. The registry describes profiling and machine learning (it names Naive Bayes classification and cluster analysis) run on linked register data. In a letter to Amnesty International before November 2024, UDK supplied its 2023 statistics for three data-driven controls. The “Really Single” model produced 412 requested cases, 292 established control cases and 135 cases with revenue (benefits stopped or reduced). “Model Abroad” (unreported departures, state and disability pension) gave 511, 351 and 36. The parental-leave controls including the “Fictitious Employment” model gave 491, 207 and 72. UDK cautioned that cases with revenue in a year are not necessarily a proportion of cases established that year. A UDK/ATP control official told Amnesty the team manages 5,000 to 6,000 cases a year, of which around 1,800 come from the models. Amnesty's report of 12 November 2024 concludes it is questionable whether the algorithms are effective. It finds most opened cases end with no further action and the system risks discrimination and mass surveillance. A Copenhagen Municipality control official said more often than not there is no fraud in the cases UDK sends. Background sources give earlier yields. AlgorithmWatch (2020) reports 2017 and 2018 controls unveiled about half a billion kroner in erroneous payments. The Automating Society 2020 Denmark chapter cites a July 2019 report. It counted 705 cases in 2017 and 1,094 in 2018 where payments were stopped, adjusted or repaid, out of 2.7 million screened beneficiaries. The dm.dk FOI report (October 2024) and ATP's page are not among the sources. The report said nearly all 1.2 million pensioners were screened and only 36 cases in 2023 ended with a benefit stopped or reduced. That matches the Model Abroad row. ATP's page credits 260 million kr. a year of savings to IT modernization generally. The 2023 figures carry no day.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The models select “requested cases” that UDK's HOK control team screens and investigates. Decisions to stop or reduce benefits are taken by humans after investigation. UDK measures model quality by the share of cases the team accepts for manual processing. Every outcome figure is a UDK statement (FOI responses and a letter) as reproduced verbatim in Amnesty International's report. No official publication of them is among the sources. Amnesty contests effectiveness and alleges discrimination risks, and UDK rejected parts of Amnesty's assessment. NNIT built the models to ATP's specifications. No developer-authored source is on record. The dm.dk report and ATP's page are not among the sources.

fields.account: Udbetaling Danmark (UDK) is the Danish public authority that has centralized welfare payments since 2012. ATP (Arbejdsmarkedets Tillaegspension) administers its benefits. ATP designs the fraud-control components of UDK's Joint Data Unit (Den Faelles Dataenhed), which was established in 2014, according to the University of Copenhagen's Offentlig AI database. NNIT A/S is the supplier. The database lists the methods run on linked register data: profiling, machine learning, Naive Bayes classification and cluster analysis. Earlier yields come from other sources. In July 2019 the Danish legal think tank Justitia used UDK figures on its data-based controls. They led to 705 cases in 2017. In 2018 they led to 1,094. Each of these cases ended with benefits stopped, changed or repaid. Its author argues that this yield is poor for data matching that can cover up to 2.7 million recipients. The authors of the Denmark chapter of Automating Society 2020 cite the July 2019 report. They give the same counts out of 2.7 million screened beneficiaries. AlgorithmWatch (2020) reports that controls in 2017 and 2018 uncovered about half a billion kroner in erroneous payments. As of 2019 UDK was reported to use up to 60 algorithms for purposes that included fraud detection. In a letter to Amnesty International before November 2024, UDK supplied its 2023 statistics for three data-driven controls. The 2023 figures carry no day. The “Really Single” model produced 412 requested cases, 292 established control cases and 135 cases with revenue (benefits stopped or reduced). “Model Abroad” (unreported departures, state and disability pension) gave 511, 351 and 36. The parental-leave controls including the “Fictitious Employment” model gave 491, 207 and 72. UDK cautioned that cases with revenue in a year are not necessarily a proportion of cases established that year. On 11 January 2024 a control official of UDK and ATP told Amnesty that the team manages 5,000 to 6,000 cases a year, of which around 1,800 come from the models. In its report of 12 November 2024, Amnesty concludes that it is questionable whether the algorithms are effective. It finds that most opened cases end with no further action. It finds that the system risks discrimination. It finds a risk of mass surveillance. A control official of Copenhagen Municipality said that more often than not there is no fraud in the cases that UDK sends. Amnesty reports that the Danish Data Protection Authority told it that the authority acts only on two grounds. One is an inquiry. The other is a complaint. No finding by a regulator on the models is on record.

fields.summary: Three of Udbetaling Danmark's machine-learning fraud models flagged cases that ended with benefits cut 135, 36 and 72 times in 2023. Amnesty International questions whether they work.
fields.account: Udbetaling Danmark (UDK) is the Danish public authority that has centralized welfare payments since 2012. ATP (Arbejdsmarkedets Tillaegspension) administers its benefits. ATP designs the fraud-control components of UDK's Joint Data Unit (Den Faelles Dataenhed), which was established in 2014, according to the University of Copenhagen's Offentlig AI database. NNIT A/S is the supplier. The database lists the methods run on linked register data: profiling, machine learning, Naive Bayes classification and cluster analysis. Earlier yields come from other sources. In July 2019 the Danish legal think tank Justitia used UDK figures on its data-based controls. They led to 705 cases in 2017. In 2018 they led to 1,094. Each of these cases ended with benefits stopped, changed or repaid. Its author argues that this yield is poor for data matching that can cover up to 2.7 million recipients. The authors of the Denmark chapter of Automating Society 2020 cite the July 2019 report. They give the same counts out of 2.7 million screened beneficiaries. AlgorithmWatch (2020) reports that controls in 2017 and 2018 uncovered about half a billion kroner in erroneous payments. As of 2019 UDK was reported to use up to 60 algorithms for purposes that included fraud detection. In a letter to Amnesty International before November 2024, UDK supplied its 2023 statistics for three data-driven controls. The 2023 figures carry no day. The “Really Single” model produced 412 requested cases, 292 established control cases and 135 cases with revenue (benefits stopped or reduced). “Model Abroad” (unreported departures, state and disability pension) gave 511, 351 and 36. The parental-leave controls including the “Fictitious Employment” model gave 491, 207 and 72. UDK cautioned that cases with revenue in a year are not necessarily a proportion of cases established that year. On 11 January 2024 a control official of UDK and ATP told Amnesty that the team manages 5,000 to 6,000 cases a year, of which around 1,800 come from the models. In its report of 12 November 2024, Amnesty concludes that it is questionable whether the algorithms are effective. It finds that most opened cases end with no further action. It finds that the system risks discrimination. It finds a risk of mass surveillance. A control official of Copenhagen Municipality said that more often than not there is no fraud in the cases that UDK sends. Amnesty reports that the Danish Data Protection Authority told it that the authority acts only on two grounds. One is an inquiry. The other is a complaint. No finding by a regulator on the models is on record.

record.title: ENEA tests machine-learning forecasts of grid failures driven by heatwaves in Italy with two universities
record.summary: With two Italian universities, ENEA tested a machine-learning model that forecasts grid failures during heatwaves. In its announcement of 18 May 2023, ENEA reports no avoided outage.
record.account: ENEA, Politecnico di Bari and Università Roma Tre tested machine-learning forecasts of heatwave-related failures in a large distribution grid in southern Italy. In its announcement of 18 May 2023, ENEA says that the model was trained on four kinds of data (failures from 2015 to 2020, temperature, humidity, energy flows). ENEA says that the model was then tested on unseen inputs. The researchers proposed that operators use the forecasts for corrective maintenance. ENEA names no utility that deployed the model. It reports no avoided outage. ENEA's Maria Valenti said that most failures in the studied network occurred at cable joints. The study appeared in IEEE Transactions on Industry Applications in 2023 under the title “A Machine Learning Approach to Fault Prediction of Power Distribution Grids under Heatwaves.” In 2025 a Politecnico di Milano team tested similar forecasts on the Milan distribution network. The cited reports do not show that the grid operator or any other utility adopted the model.

evidence.quote: This study introduces a novel machine learning methodology to enhance grid resilience during heatwaves, focusing on fault prediction and heatwave forecasting. Three complementary approaches were systematically evaluated: Ridge Regression with Recursive Feature Elimination and Cross-Validation, Random Forest Regression, and Second-order Polynomial Poisson Regression with Recursive Feature Elimination and Cross-Validation.

fields.summary: With two Italian universities, ENEA tested a machine-learning model that forecasts grid failures during heatwaves. In its announcement of 18 May 2023, ENEA reports no avoided outage.
fields.account: ENEA, Politecnico di Bari and Università Roma Tre tested machine-learning forecasts of heatwave-related failures in a large distribution grid in southern Italy. In its announcement of 18 May 2023, ENEA says that the model was trained on four kinds of data (failures from 2015 to 2020, temperature, humidity, energy flows). ENEA says that the model was then tested on unseen inputs. The researchers proposed that operators use the forecasts for corrective maintenance. ENEA names no utility that deployed the model. It reports no avoided outage. ENEA's Maria Valenti said that most failures in the studied network occurred at cable joints. The study appeared in IEEE Transactions on Industry Applications in 2023 under the title “A Machine Learning Approach to Fault Prediction of Power Distribution Grids under Heatwaves.” In 2025 a Politecnico di Milano team tested similar forecasts on the Milan distribution network. The cited reports do not show that the grid operator or any other utility adopted the model.

record.title: A CIA tool called “Ghost Murmur”, pairing quantum magnetometry with AI, may have located downed F-15E officer “Dude 44 Bravo” in Iran before his rescue in April 2026, but CBS later reports that unnamed CIA technology pinpointed him
record.summary: Two anonymous sources credit the CIA's Ghost Murmur, quantum sensing paired with AI, with locating a downed F-15E officer in Iran. CBS reports that CIA technology pinpointed him. It names no tool.
record.account: The White House briefing of 6 April 2026 documents the rescue of the downed F-15E weapons systems officer in Iran. In the official transcript, the speakers describe watching his suspected position with a camera from 40 miles away. That distance concerns the camera. No source establishes a range for detecting a heartbeat. On 7 April the New York Post reported that two anonymous sources attributed the officer's location to a Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) tool called Ghost Murmur. They described quantum magnetic sensing combined with AI that separates a heartbeat signal from background noise. They attributed its development to Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works. Lockheed Martin declined to comment. In a telephone interview with the Post on 8 April, President Trump called the tool important to the rescue but supplied no technical explanation. The Post and Scientific American separately interviewed physicists who questioned the described capability. Ghost Murmur is not named in the official briefing. The briefing establishes no contribution by AI. No public measurements establish that the claimed system located the officer. No inspectable technical account establishes it. On 13 September 2026, 60 Minutes reported from its own interviews that the CIA used top-secret technology to pinpoint the officer's location. CBS did not name Ghost Murmur. It did not say that the technology used AI. Admiral Brad Cooper told CBS that messages from the officer, including “I'm hurt, I'm moving”, reached US forces. The officer said that he carried communication equipment. He said that he did not immediately use it. The documented outcome is one rescued airman, with the claimed AI contribution unverified.

display.answer: The claim about Ghost Murmur traces to two anonymous sources in the New York Post and to President Trump's telephone interview with the same paper. The White House transcript documents the rescue. The Post and Scientific American interviewed physicists separately. CBS reports from its own interviews with the officer and with officials.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: Two anonymous sources credit the CIA's Ghost Murmur, quantum sensing paired with AI, with locating a downed F-15E officer in Iran. CBS reports that CIA technology pinpointed him. It names no tool.
fields.account: The White House briefing of 6 April 2026 documents the rescue of the downed F-15E weapons systems officer in Iran. In the official transcript, the speakers describe watching his suspected position with a camera from 40 miles away. That distance concerns the camera. No source establishes a range for detecting a heartbeat. On 7 April the New York Post reported that two anonymous sources attributed the officer's location to a Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) tool called Ghost Murmur. They described quantum magnetic sensing combined with AI that separates a heartbeat signal from background noise. They attributed its development to Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works. Lockheed Martin declined to comment. In a telephone interview with the Post on 8 April, President Trump called the tool important to the rescue but supplied no technical explanation. The Post and Scientific American separately interviewed physicists who questioned the described capability. Ghost Murmur is not named in the official briefing. The briefing establishes no contribution by AI. No public measurements establish that the claimed system located the officer. No inspectable technical account establishes it. On 13 September 2026, 60 Minutes reported from its own interviews that the CIA used top-secret technology to pinpoint the officer's location. CBS did not name Ghost Murmur. It did not say that the technology used AI. Admiral Brad Cooper told CBS that messages from the officer, including “I'm hurt, I'm moving”, reached US forces. The officer said that he carried communication equipment. He said that he did not immediately use it. The documented outcome is one rescued airman, with the claimed AI contribution unverified.

record.title: A suicide alert from Meta, routed to Uttar Pradesh Police, brings officers to a 25-year-old in Meerut within eight minutes
record.summary: After Meta alerted police to a 25-year-old man's video on Instagram, officers in Meerut reached his home within eight minutes. His condition improved after treatment in hospital.
record.account: On 7 June 2026 a 25-year-old man from the Sardhana area of Meerut, Uttar Pradesh, posted an Instagram video. In it he appeared to drink a white liquid. Police said that Meta sent a suicide alert about the post to the Social Media Center at Uttar Pradesh Police headquarters at 6:53 pm. The center alerted Meerut Police. Then a Sardhana team reached his home within eight minutes. They found him in a critical condition with a bottle of suspected liquid nearby. They took him to hospital, where his condition improved after treatment. He told police that he was under stress following the end of a relationship. According to police data that the Press Trust of India cited, such alerts saved 3,011 lives statewide from 1 January 2023 to 31 May 2026. On 6 January 2026 Decode reported its own interviews with Uttar Pradesh officers. They described rescues. One alert that they described was a false alarm. The outlet noted that Meta publishes no data on false positives for India. On 22 October 2026 the Times of India reported that police credit the alerts with more than 4,000 lives saved from 1 January 2023 to 10 October 2026.

fields.account: On 7 June 2026 a 25-year-old man from the Sardhana area of Meerut, Uttar Pradesh, posted an Instagram video. In it he appeared to drink a white liquid. Police said that Meta sent a suicide alert about the post to the Social Media Center at Uttar Pradesh Police headquarters at 6:53 pm. The center alerted Meerut Police. Then a Sardhana team reached his home within eight minutes. They found him in a critical condition with a bottle of suspected liquid nearby. They took him to hospital, where his condition improved after treatment. He told police that he was under stress following the end of a relationship. According to police data that the Press Trust of India cited, such alerts saved 3,011 lives statewide from 1 January 2023 to 31 May 2026. On 6 January 2026 Decode reported its own interviews with Uttar Pradesh officers. They described rescues. One alert that they described was a false alarm. The outlet noted that Meta publishes no data on false positives for India. On 22 October 2026 the Times of India reported that police credit the alerts with more than 4,000 lives saved from 1 January 2023 to 10 October 2026.

record.summary: Meta's system for detecting suicide risk flagged an 18-year-old's Instagram post for review. Raebareli police reached him within 12 minutes. He was treated after taking rat poison.
record.account: On 29 March 2026 an 18-year-old class 12 student from Raebareli, Uttar Pradesh, texted his girlfriend “Alvida” after a breakup. He lived within the Mill Area police station limits. He posted a suicide video on Instagram with rat poison. The post carried messages of intent. At about 8:58 pm Meta picked out the content. It emailed an alert to the Social Media Center at Uttar Pradesh Police headquarters. The center traced his mobile number. It traced his location. It alerted Raebareli police. A police team reached his home within 12 minutes. They found him in severe distress, with an empty rat-poison packet nearby. Police and family took him to a nearby hospital, where he was treated. On 1 April 2026 police said that he was stable. A similar rescue after a Meta alert followed in Meerut in June 2026. In October 2026 one followed in Gorakhpur. The Times of India reported on 22 October 2026 that Uttar Pradesh Police say that they saved more than 4,000 lives from 1 January 2023 to 10 October 2026 by responding to alerts linked to suicide-related posts. According to Decode, the arrangement with Meta has been in place since 2022.

record.brief: The Raebareli rescue preceded a similar rescue in Meerut in June 2026. Both took place under an arrangement in which Meta has alerted the Uttar Pradesh Police since 2022.[1] On 29 March 2026 an 18-year-old posted a suicide video on Instagram. Meta flagged it at about 8:58 pm and emailed the Social Media Center at Uttar Pradesh Police headquarters. The center traced his phone number and location and alerted Raebareli police. A team reached his home within 12 minutes and found an empty packet of rat poison. Police and family took him to a hospital. On 1 April 2026 police said that he was stable.[2] None of the sources says whether Meta’s classifier or a user report first flagged the post.[3] No clinician is quoted, and the type of rat poison is not reported. The claim that his life was saved therefore rests on the police account.[4] Meta’s figure for faster escalation is self-reported and dates from November 2017. At that time, the company said that reports accelerated by pattern recognition were escalated to local authorities twice as quickly as other reports.[5]

fields.account: On 29 March 2026 an 18-year-old class 12 student from Raebareli, Uttar Pradesh, texted his girlfriend “Alvida” after a breakup. He lived within the Mill Area police station limits. He posted a suicide video on Instagram with rat poison. The post carried messages of intent. At about 8:58 pm Meta picked out the content. It emailed an alert to the Social Media Center at Uttar Pradesh Police headquarters. The center traced his mobile number. It traced his location. It alerted Raebareli police. A police team reached his home within 12 minutes. They found him in severe distress, with an empty rat-poison packet nearby. Police and family took him to a nearby hospital, where he was treated. On 1 April 2026 police said that he was stable. A similar rescue after a Meta alert followed in Meerut in June 2026. In October 2026 one followed in Gorakhpur. The Times of India reported on 22 October 2026 that Uttar Pradesh Police say that they saved more than 4,000 lives from 1 January 2023 to 10 October 2026 by responding to alerts linked to suicide-related posts. According to Decode, the arrangement with Meta has been in place since 2022.

details.value: Hanoi's Traffic Police run the AI traffic-camera system, in VOV's words, “to ensure security and order and support the people” as well as to manage traffic. VOV reported that it has 1,837 cameras with signals controlled by AI and was due to enter official operation in December 2025. Tracing a lost resident for a search by the ward police falls within that remit.

details.label: Contribution of the AI
details.value: The system's contribution was the trace. Police searched it in the direction that the family gave. It returned images of the man walking along Nguyễn Tuân street toward Thanh Xuân Park and across other streets. That gave the police a route and pictures for a public appeal. A passing resident found him in Dịch Vọng about six hours and 45 minutes after the report. No police statement shows that the finder had seen the appeal or that officers reached him. So the discovery itself cannot be credited to the system. The vendor is not named, and every account comes from the police.

record.title: Hanoi traffic police trace a missing 78-year-old on the city's new AI cameras before a passer-by finds him hypoglycemic at 3 a.m. in Dịch Vọng
record.summary: Hanoi police traced a lost 78-year-old on AI traffic cameras on 15 December 2025. A passer-by who found him at 3 a.m. the next day took him home.
record.account: Hanoi's AI traffic-camera network began official operation on 13 December 2025. A 78-year-old man from Thanh Xuân ward, Hanoi, went out to exercise at 3:30 p.m. on 15 December 2025. He did not return. At 8:15 p.m. his family reported him to Thanh Xuân Ward Police. Ward officers worked with the Hanoi Traffic Police Department. Major Nguyễn Tá Khanh's team there searched the AI traffic-camera system in the direction that the family gave. It traced him along Nguyễn Tuân street toward Thanh Xuân Park and other streets. VietNamNet and Tiền Phong say that the images were posted on social media. At about 3 a.m. on 16 December a passing resident found him in Dịch Vọng. He was hypoglycemic. He was close to fainting. The resident took him home. The police have not linked the finder to the camera trace. They have not linked him to the appeal on social media. Sức khỏe & Đời sống reports that the family said that his health was stable. It reports that they sent thanks to the police and residents. By 29 June 2026 Hanoi had nearly 5,000 AI cameras.

data.retained_case_account: A 78-year-old man from Thanh Xuân ward, Hanoi, went out to exercise at 3:30 p.m. on 15 December 2025 and did not return. At 8:15 p.m. his family reported him to Thanh Xuân Ward Police. Ward officers worked with the Hanoi Traffic Police Department. Major Nguyễn Tá Khanh's team there searched the AI traffic-camera system in the direction the family gave. It traced him along Nguyễn Tuân street toward Thanh Xuân Park and other streets. VietNamNet and Tiền Phong say the images were posted on social media. At about 3 a.m. on 16 December a passing resident found him in Dịch Vọng, hypoglycemic and close to fainting, and took him home. No source links the finder to the appeal.

fields.summary: Hanoi police traced a lost 78-year-old on AI traffic cameras on 15 December 2025. A passer-by who found him at 3 a.m. the next day took him home.
fields.account: Hanoi's AI traffic-camera network began official operation on 13 December 2025. A 78-year-old man from Thanh Xuân ward, Hanoi, went out to exercise at 3:30 p.m. on 15 December 2025. He did not return. At 8:15 p.m. his family reported him to Thanh Xuân Ward Police. Ward officers worked with the Hanoi Traffic Police Department. Major Nguyễn Tá Khanh's team there searched the AI traffic-camera system in the direction that the family gave. It traced him along Nguyễn Tuân street toward Thanh Xuân Park and other streets. VietNamNet and Tiền Phong say that the images were posted on social media. At about 3 a.m. on 16 December a passing resident found him in Dịch Vọng. He was hypoglycemic. He was close to fainting. The resident took him home. The police have not linked the finder to the camera trace. They have not linked him to the appeal on social media. Sức khỏe & Đời sống reports that the family said that his health was stable. It reports that they sent thanks to the police and residents. By 29 June 2026 Hanoi had nearly 5,000 AI cameras.

record.title: The Kamrup Express stops short of about 60 elephants in Assam after an AI detection system alerts its crew, who also see the herd
record.summary: On 16 October 2024 Northeast Frontier Railway's AI-based Intrusion Detection System alerted the crew of the Kamrup Express, who also saw about 60 elephants crossing in Assam. The crew braked.
record.account: On 16 October 2024 at about 8:37 p.m., train 15959 Kamrup Express was running from Guwahati toward Lumding. It neared a herd of about 60 wild elephants crossing the track between Habaipur and Lamsakhang stations in Assam. Northeast Frontier Railway said that loco pilot J.D. Das and assistant loco pilot Umesh Kumar noticed the herd. It said that they applied the emergency brake. It said that the AI-based Intrusion Detection System operating on that section also alerted the drivers. That system uses existing optical fibers as sensors to identify the movements of animals. Its alerts go to control offices. Station masters get them. Gatemen get them. Loco pilots get them. The train stopped. No collision occurred. Northeast Frontier Railway reported that it saved 414 elephants in 2023 and 383 up to 16 October 2024. By December 2025 the system covered 141 route kilometers of Northeast Frontier Railway. Tenders had been awarded for 981 more route kilometers nationwide. On 20 December 2025 a Rajdhani Express killed seven elephants at Sangjurai, about 30 kilometers away, where the railway said that no such system was installed. The Times of India reported on 21 December 2025 that the system runs on the Habaipur to Lumding section. The paper reported that it covers about 70 kilometers of track in Assam. On 8 October 2026 The Sentinel reported that the railway counted 255 elephants protected in 2026 across four divisions.

data.retained_case_account: On 16 October 2024 at about 8:37 pm, train 15959 Kamrup Express was running from Guwahati toward Lumding. It neared a herd of about 60 wild elephants crossing the track between Habaipur and Lamsakhang stations in Assam. Northeast Frontier Railway said loco pilot J.D. Das and assistant loco pilot Umesh Kumar noticed the herd and applied the emergency brake. It said the AI-based Intrusion Detection System operating on that section also alerted the drivers. That system uses existing optical fibers as sensors to identify animal movements and alert control offices, station masters, gatemen and loco pilots. The train stopped and no collision occurred. NFR reported it saved 414 elephants in 2023 and 383 up to 16 October 2024.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The operator's release says the drivers noticed the herd and applied the emergency brake and were “also alerted” by the IDS. One local report says the braking followed the IDS warning. The AI alert is documented, but its share of the causal credit is not separable from the crew's own sighting. Hence protective response, prevention unproven.
