fields.account: On 16 October 2024 at about 8:37 p.m., train 15959 Kamrup Express was running from Guwahati toward Lumding. It neared a herd of about 60 wild elephants crossing the track between Habaipur and Lamsakhang stations in Assam. Northeast Frontier Railway said that loco pilot J.D. Das and assistant loco pilot Umesh Kumar noticed the herd. It said that they applied the emergency brake. It said that the AI-based Intrusion Detection System operating on that section also alerted the drivers. That system uses existing optical fibers as sensors to identify the movements of animals. Its alerts go to control offices. Station masters get them. Gatemen get them. Loco pilots get them. The train stopped. No collision occurred. Northeast Frontier Railway reported that it saved 414 elephants in 2023 and 383 up to 16 October 2024. By December 2025 the system covered 141 route kilometers of Northeast Frontier Railway. Tenders had been awarded for 981 more route kilometers nationwide. On 20 December 2025 a Rajdhani Express killed seven elephants at Sangjurai, about 30 kilometers away, where the railway said that no such system was installed. The Times of India reported on 21 December 2025 that the system runs on the Habaipur to Lumding section. The paper reported that it covers about 70 kilometers of track in Assam. On 8 October 2026 The Sentinel reported that the railway counted 255 elephants protected in 2026 across four divisions.

record.title: Homeland Security Investigations' Operation Renewed Hope uses facial recognition to identify 311 probable child victims in cold cases. It also uses AI to enhance images
record.summary: U.S.-led investigators credited facial recognition, reportedly Clearview AI, for leads in a 2023 operation that made 311 probable identifications of child abuse victims. AI image enhancement helped.
record.account: Operation Renewed Hope began on 17 July 2023. The Cyber Crimes Center of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) hosted investigators from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the U.S. Marshals, Interpol, Europol and 13 foreign agencies. They reviewed series of child sexual abuse material in which the victims had not been identified. On 9 August 2023 U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) reported 311 probable identifications of previously unknown victims, 14 positive contacts and several confirmed rescues from active abuse. More than 100 leads went to field offices. Leads went to 25 countries. Arrests had already been made in the United States and Canada. The ICE release does not mention artificial intelligence (AI). NBC News reports that HSI officials credited new facial recognition and artificial intelligence technology for fresh leads. Mike Prado of HSI described images enhanced with AI as a starting point for investigation. He said the same of images enhanced with machine learning. Forbes reports that officials did not confirm Clearview or any specific program. On 24 August 2023 ABC (Australia) reported that the operation used Clearview AI's facial recognition alongside other techniques, citing Scott Anderson, an analyst with Queensland Police. Crikey reported on 25 January 2024 that the operation ran from 17 July to 4 August 2023. Drawing on internal police correspondence and a statement from the Australian Federal Police (AFP), Crikey reported that Australian case material was analyzed with Clearview AI, which the AFP was not allowed to use.

record.brief: Operation Renewed Hope ran from 17 July 2023 into early August at the Cyber Crimes Center of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI). U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) reported 311 probable identifications of previously unknown child victims. It also reported several confirmed rescues from active abuse. Arrests had already been made in the United States and Canada.[1] The case bears on the argument over police use of facial recognition. AI's part in it is hard to weigh. ICE did not mention AI in its release. NBC News reported that new facial recognition and artificial intelligence technology had produced fresh leads in formerly cold cases. Mike Prado of HSI spoke of images enhanced with AI or machine learning. He said that they can give investigators a starting point.[2] ABC News in Australia reported that Clearview AI's facial recognition was used. Forbes reported that officials did not confirm Clearview or any specific program.[3] Crikey reported on 25 January 2024 that Australian case material had been analyzed with Clearview AI. The Australian Federal Police was not allowed to use that software.[4] The outcomes are ICE's count. No figure shows how many identifications came from the tools and how many from manual work. In a separate case in Finland, police were reportedly reprimanded. A unit of the National Bureau of Investigation had allegedly used Clearview AI to identify potential abuse victims.

fields.account: Operation Renewed Hope began on 17 July 2023. The Cyber Crimes Center of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) hosted investigators from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the U.S. Marshals, Interpol, Europol and 13 foreign agencies. They reviewed series of child sexual abuse material in which the victims had not been identified. On 9 August 2023 U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) reported 311 probable identifications of previously unknown victims, 14 positive contacts and several confirmed rescues from active abuse. More than 100 leads went to field offices. Leads went to 25 countries. Arrests had already been made in the United States and Canada. The ICE release does not mention artificial intelligence (AI). NBC News reports that HSI officials credited new facial recognition and artificial intelligence technology for fresh leads. Mike Prado of HSI described images enhanced with AI as a starting point for investigation. He said the same of images enhanced with machine learning. Forbes reports that officials did not confirm Clearview or any specific program. On 24 August 2023 ABC (Australia) reported that the operation used Clearview AI's facial recognition alongside other techniques, citing Scott Anderson, an analyst with Queensland Police. Crikey reported on 25 January 2024 that the operation ran from 17 July to 4 August 2023. Drawing on internal police correspondence and a statement from the Australian Federal Police (AFP), Crikey reported that Australian case material was analyzed with Clearview AI, which the AFP was not allowed to use.

fields.account: Operation Renewed Hope began on 17 July 2023. The Cyber Crimes Center of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) hosted investigators from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the U.S. Marshals, Interpol, Europol and 13 foreign agencies. They reviewed series of child sexual abuse material in which the victims had not been identified. On 9 August 2023 U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) reported 311 probable identifications of previously unknown victims, 14 positive contacts and several confirmed rescues from active abuse. More than 100 leads went to field offices. Leads went to 25 countries. Arrests had already been made in the United States and Canada. The ICE release does not mention artificial intelligence (AI). NBC News reports that HSI officials credited new facial recognition and artificial intelligence technology for fresh leads. Mike Prado of HSI described images enhanced with AI as a starting point for investigation. He said the same of images enhanced with machine learning. Forbes reports that officials did not confirm Clearview or any specific program. On 24 August 2023 ABC (Australia) reported that the operation used Clearview AI's facial recognition alongside other techniques, citing Scott Anderson, an analyst with Queensland Police. Crikey reported on 25 January 2024 that the operation ran from 17 July to 4 August 2023. Drawing on internal police correspondence and a statement from the Australian Federal Police (AFP), Crikey reported that Australian case material was analyzed with Clearview AI, which the AFP was not allowed to use.

details.value: The Turkish National Police built ASENA (Analiz Sistemleri Narkotik Ağı) to find and investigate drug crime in linked police and court databases, and it has been in use since March 2021. Police in Hakkari treated the flagged car as a suspected drug shipment, and officers found explosives instead. So this benefit lay outside what the system was built for.

details.label: Contribution of the AI
details.value: The program supplied the lead and nothing more. The minister said that the analysis programs, “what they call artificial intelligence”, had flagged a suspicious vehicle thought to be carrying drugs. The Hakkari police chief called him on the evening of 20 March. Officers then stopped the car at a fixed checkpoint, searched the concealed compartment and arrested the driver. Prosecutors and the court did the rest. Neither the minister nor the police describe the program's inputs or the data that it matched, or say whether an analyst reviewed the flag before the stop. The defendant spoke in court of “those who informed”, but no informant appears in the sources.

record.title: ASENA analysis program flags a car at Yüksekova carrying 52.5 kg of explosives bound for Istanbul
record.summary: The Turkish police's ASENA analysis program flagged a car at Yüksekova on 20 March 2022. Officers found 52.5 kg of explosives. The interior minister said that they were bound for Istanbul.
record.account: On 20 March 2022 at about 19:00, officers of the Hakkari Provincial Police Directorate stopped a car at the Yüksekova-Van checkpoint exit in Yüksekova, Turkey. Work on the directorate's ASENA analysis program had flagged it as suspicious, initially as a suspected drug shipment. A search of a hidden compartment under the spare-wheel well found 133 packets, 52.5 kg, of factory-made explosive assessed as PETN-RDX. Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu said on 21 March that the target was Istanbul. The driver, A.K., a police officer posted in Istanbul, was remanded on 22 March 2022. In a June 2022 interview with Anadolu Ajansı, İbrahim Seydioğulları, head of the police Narcotics Crimes Department, listed the 52 kg of explosives among the finds of operations that he said had started with ASENA. On 20 November 2023 the Hakkari 2nd Heavy Penal Court sentenced A.K. to 21 years in prison for supplying weapons to a terrorist organization. Four co-defendants got 17.5 years each.

Work on the directorate's ASENA analysis program had flagged the car. A hidden compartment under the spare-wheel well held 133 packets of factory-made explosive, 52.5 kg in all. On 20 November 2023 the Hakkari 2nd Heavy Penal Court sentenced him to 21 years in prison for supplying weapons to a terrorist organization. It sentenced four co-defendants to 17.5 years each for the same offense.[2] ASENA was designed to flag drug crime. This find lay outside its purpose. He listed the explosives among the finds of operations that, by his account, had started with ASENA.[4] No source records the data that ASENA matched for this car. data.retained_case_account: On 20 March 2022 at about 19:00, officers of the Hakkari Provincial Police Directorate stopped a car at the Yüksekova-Van checkpoint exit in Yüksekova, Turkey. Work on the directorate's ASENA analysis program had flagged it as suspicious, initially as a suspected drug shipment. A search of a hidden compartment under the spare-wheel well found 133 packets, 52.5 kg, of factory-made explosive assessed as PETN-RDX. The driver, A.K., a police officer posted in Istanbul, was remanded on 22 March 2022. Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu said on 21 March that the target was Istanbul. On 20 November 2023 the Hakkari 2nd Heavy Penal Court gave A.K. 21 years for supplying weapons to a terrorist organization. Four co-defendants got 17.5 years each.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The program supplied the lead and nothing more. The minister said the analysis programs, “what they call artificial intelligence”, had identified a suspicious vehicle thought to be carrying drugs. The Hakkari police chief called him on the evening of 20 March. Officers then stopped the car at a fixed checkpoint, searched the concealed compartment and arrested the driver; prosecutors and the court did the rest. No source describes the program's inputs, the data it matched, or whether an analyst reviewed the flag before the stop. The defendant spoke in court of “those who informed”, but no source reports an informant.

The court convicted five men of supplying weapons to a terrorist organization. The harm averted could have been an attack with many casualties, though reporters did not establish the plan.
The Hakkari police got a lead that ended in a seizure, five arrests and five convictions. The minister counted it among 15 similar actions that police had stopped that year.

fields.purpose: The Turkish National Police built ASENA (Analiz Sistemleri Narkotik Ağı) to find and investigate drug crime in linked police and court databases, and it has been in use since March 2021. Police in Hakkari treated the flagged car as a suspected drug shipment, and officers found explosives instead. So this benefit lay outside what the system was built for.

fields.account: On 20 March 2022 at about 19:00, officers of the Hakkari Provincial Police Directorate stopped a car at the Yüksekova-Van checkpoint exit in Yüksekova, Turkey. Work on the directorate's ASENA analysis program had flagged it as suspicious, initially as a suspected drug shipment. A search of a hidden compartment under the spare-wheel well found 133 packets, 52.5 kg, of factory-made explosive assessed as PETN-RDX. Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu said on 21 March that the target was Istanbul. The driver, A.K., a police officer posted in Istanbul, was remanded on 22 March 2022. In a June 2022 interview with Anadolu Ajansı, İbrahim Seydioğulları, head of the police Narcotics Crimes Department, listed the 52 kg of explosives among the finds of operations that he said had started with ASENA. On 20 November 2023 the Hakkari 2nd Heavy Penal Court sentenced A.K. to 21 years in prison for supplying weapons to a terrorist organization. Four co-defendants got 17.5 years each.

record.account: Thorn's chief executive, Julie Cordua, recounted this rescue at an Amazon conference in Las Vegas. WIRED's Tom Simonite quoted her on 19 June 2019. The source places it in April 2019 without a day. Cordua said that a California law enforcement officer had screenshotted a missing child's picture from a post by the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. The officer ran it through Spotlight, Thorn's investigator tool that matches faces and other clues in online sex ads. Using Amazon's facial recognition, Spotlight returned a list of ads featuring the girl, who had been sold for weeks. More traditional police work followed. Cordua said that the child was recovered within weeks. No police record of this rescue is among the sources. The sources include no court record of it. Snopes had reported on 4 September 2018 that Thorn's 2017 impact report claimed that its tools helped identify 5,791 child victims and rescue 103. Snopes notes that the figures come from Thorn's surveys of police users. It notes that viral claims conflated identification with rescue. On 10 May 2024 Thorn announced that it was moving Spotlight to a new home led by its former Vice President of Victim Identification, Kristin Boorse. Canary NGO Ltd now builds the tool. It says that more than 8,000 investigators use it.

record.title: OpenAI alert relayed through the FBI leads Espírito Santo police to detain a father a day before his stated date to kill his son
record.summary: OpenAI's safety systems flagged a ChatGPT user's plan to kill his 8-year-old son. Alerted through the FBI, Brazilian police held him a day before his stated date.
record.account: In 2026 a 36-year-old farmer in São Gabriel da Palha, Espírito Santo, Brazil, told ChatGPT about a plan to kill his 8-year-old son. He said that he had offered R$50,000 to a hitman. He said that he had set 20 June as the date. OpenAI's safety systems picked out the account. The company referred it to the FBI. The FBI passed it to the Ministry of Justice's CyberLab. The Polícia Civil do Espírito Santo received it on 16 June. It arrested him under warrants on 19 June. Officers seized his phone. They seized four bottles of an unidentified substance. They seized a knotted rope. He admitted the searches but denied intent. He was freed on habeas corpus on 13 August 2026 after 54 days. He wore an ankle monitor. A no-contact order applied to him. The inquiry continues. BBC News Brasil reported on 14 August 2026 that the court freed him because the inquiry had run too long without a charge. Legal experts whom BBC News Brasil interviewed said that the messages justified pretrial detention. They said that the messages alone would not support a charge. The lead investigator told BBC News Brasil that OpenAI sent the user's prompts without ChatGPT's replies. In early October 2026, Folha reported, OpenAI closed an account and sent its data to Brazil's federal police in an inquiry into ChatGPT users who threatened President Lula. The report does not say whose account it was. The company passed the data to the Federal Police.
record.purpose: OpenAI built its moderation layer to send conversations that show plans to harm others to human reviewers. Under a policy published on 26 August 2025, those reviewers may refer an imminent threat to law enforcement. The referral that led to the arrest came from that layer working as built.
record.system: ChatGPT with OpenAI's safety-monitoring pipeline (automated classifiers plus human review and law-enforcement referral)
record.deployer: OpenAI

ratings.reason: The 8-year-old, and his mother who was placed under a no-contact order, were shielded from a plan that the father had dated to 20 June. Police say that the platform's information was corroborated when they arrived. He denies intent and no charge has been filed, so a life-saving effect is not established.

The Polícia Civil do Espírito Santo obtained a lead through the FBI and the Ministry of Justice CyberLab. It says that it had no other way to get it. Its cybercrime chief called the alert another path for police work. The Ministry rated it the gravest of three such alerts in Brazil.

display.answer: The police release and the Brazilian news reports of 25 to 27 June 2026 cover the same chain. It ran from OpenAI to the FBI, the Ministry of Justice's CyberLab and the state police, and g1 cites the deputy police chief. BBC News Brasil adds the court's release, the views of legal experts and the lead investigator's account of what OpenAI sent. OpenAI describes the referral process on its policy page of 26 August 2025 and does not mention this case.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: OpenAI's safety systems flagged a ChatGPT user's plan to kill his 8-year-old son. Alerted through the FBI, Brazilian police held him a day before his stated date.
fields.account: In 2026 a 36-year-old farmer in São Gabriel da Palha, Espírito Santo, Brazil, told ChatGPT about a plan to kill his 8-year-old son. He said that he had offered R$50,000 to a hitman. He said that he had set 20 June as the date. OpenAI's safety systems picked out the account. The company referred it to the FBI. The FBI passed it to the Ministry of Justice's CyberLab. The Polícia Civil do Espírito Santo received it on 16 June. It arrested him under warrants on 19 June. Officers seized his phone. They seized four bottles of an unidentified substance. They seized a knotted rope. He admitted the searches but denied intent. He was freed on habeas corpus on 13 August 2026 after 54 days. He wore an ankle monitor. A no-contact order applied to him. The inquiry continues. BBC News Brasil reported on 14 August 2026 that the court freed him because the inquiry had run too long without a charge. Legal experts whom BBC News Brasil interviewed said that the messages justified pretrial detention. They said that the messages alone would not support a charge. The lead investigator told BBC News Brasil that OpenAI sent the user's prompts without ChatGPT's replies. In early October 2026, Folha reported, OpenAI closed an account and sent its data to Brazil's federal police in an inquiry into ChatGPT users who threatened President Lula. The report does not say whose account it was. The company passed the data to the Federal Police.

record.title: Saronic's Corsair sea drone carries two Apache crew members off Oman to a helicopter hoist
record.summary: A remotely piloted Saronic Corsair sea drone carried two Apache crew off Oman to a helicopter hoist. Central Command reported that both were rescued within approximately two hours.
record.account: U.S. Central Command reported that two Army AH-64 Apache crew members were rescued at 7:33 p.m. Eastern time on 8 June 2026. That was 3:33 a.m. on 9 June in Oman. That time marks the rescue and is distinct from the time that the helicopter went down. Central Command said that both were rescued within approximately two hours. It said that they were stable. In its release, Central Command said that the cause of the helicopter’s loss was under investigation. In a direct interview with DefenseScoop, Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Central Command, identified the vessel as a Saronic Corsair operated by the Navy’s Task Force 59. He said that it picked up the crew. He said that it carried them to another point on the water for a helicopter hoist. Al-Monitor reported on 10 June 2026 that military officials told U.S. media that an operator piloted the Corsair from afar. Stars and Stripes reported the same day that the vessel was guided to the site. It reported that the vessel located the soldiers. It reported that the vessel carried them to safer waters. Mark Cancian of the Center for Strategic and International Studies told the paper that a drone gives the same capability at less risk than a crewed platform. Which functions of the vessel ran on their own during the rescue has not been reported. On 18 September 2026, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Saronic employees that the pilots are alive because of the vessel. No finding on the cause of the helicopter's loss has been published.

The Navy has reported no outcome for the military beyond the recovery of the two crew members. The lower risk to crewed rescuers rests on an analyst's general statement, so the extent of any benefit to the organization cannot be established.

data.answer:
A Navy Corsair sea drone picked up two Apache crew off Oman and carried them to a helicopter hoist; CENTCOM reported that both were rescued within about two hours.

Hawkins identified an unmanned Corsair as the recovery vessel. DefenseScoop describes the platform’s autonomous capabilities, but its suggestion that passive sensing helped locate the crew is an inference. The official sources do not identify the navigation mode, human supervision, or sensor contribution during this rescue. A crewed helicopter completed the recovery.

data.retained_case_account: U.S. Central Command reported that two Army AH-64 Apache crew members were rescued at 7:33 p.m. Eastern time on June 8, 2026, or 3:33 a.m. on June 9 in Oman. That is the rescue time, not the time that the helicopter went down. CENTCOM said that recovery took approximately two hours and that both crew members were stable. In a direct interview with DefenseScoop, Capt. Tim Hawkins identified the vessel as a Saronic Corsair operated by the Navy’s Task Force 59. He said that it picked up the crew and carried them to another point on the water for a helicopter hoist. The official release said that the cause of the helicopter’s loss was under investigation. The sources do not identify which autonomous functions were used during the rescue.

fields.account: U.S. Central Command reported that two Army AH-64 Apache crew members were rescued at 7:33 p.m. Eastern time on 8 June 2026. That was 3:33 a.m. on 9 June in Oman. That time marks the rescue and is distinct from the time that the helicopter went down. Central Command said that both were rescued within approximately two hours. It said that they were stable. In its release, Central Command said that the cause of the helicopter’s loss was under investigation. In a direct interview with DefenseScoop, Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Central Command, identified the vessel as a Saronic Corsair operated by the Navy’s Task Force 59. He said that it picked up the crew. He said that it carried them to another point on the water for a helicopter hoist. Al-Monitor reported on 10 June 2026 that military officials told U.S. media that an operator piloted the Corsair from afar. Stars and Stripes reported the same day that the vessel was guided to the site. It reported that the vessel located the soldiers. It reported that the vessel carried them to safer waters. Mark Cancian of the Center for Strategic and International Studies told the paper that a drone gives the same capability at less risk than a crewed platform. Which functions of the vessel ran on their own during the rescue has not been reported. On 18 September 2026, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Saronic employees that the pilots are alive because of the vessel. No finding on the cause of the helicopter's loss has been published.

fields.summary: A remotely piloted Saronic Corsair sea drone carried two Apache crew off Oman to a helicopter hoist. Central Command reported that both were rescued within approximately two hours.
fields.account: U.S. Central Command reported that two Army AH-64 Apache crew members were rescued at 7:33 p.m. Eastern time on 8 June 2026. That was 3:33 a.m. on 9 June in Oman. That time marks the rescue and is distinct from the time that the helicopter went down. Central Command said that both were rescued within approximately two hours. It said that they were stable. In its release, Central Command said that the cause of the helicopter’s loss was under investigation. In a direct interview with DefenseScoop, Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Central Command, identified the vessel as a Saronic Corsair operated by the Navy’s Task Force 59. He said that it picked up the crew. He said that it carried them to another point on the water for a helicopter hoist. Al-Monitor reported on 10 June 2026 that military officials told U.S. media that an operator piloted the Corsair from afar. Stars and Stripes reported the same day that the vessel was guided to the site. It reported that the vessel located the soldiers. It reported that the vessel carried them to safer waters. Mark Cancian of the Center for Strategic and International Studies told the paper that a drone gives the same capability at less risk than a crewed platform. Which functions of the vessel ran on their own during the rescue has not been reported. On 18 September 2026, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Saronic employees that the pilots are alive because of the vessel. No finding on the cause of the helicopter's loss has been published.

record.summary: Asilla says that its behavior-analysis AI for security cameras alerted guards, who reached two people at apparent risk of suicide. The facilities are undisclosed. The dates are undisclosed.
record.account: Tokyo-based Asilla's system assesses the likelihood that a person will jump by analyzing behavior on security-camera footage. Asilla says that it has trained the system since 2022 with around 200 facilities on about seven million pieces of footage. In a product release of 26 January 2024, Asilla describes a function in AI Security asilla version 2.4 that detects the risk of a jump. It uses the trajectories of movement. It uses position. It uses patterns of body motion. The system looks for pacing near a platform edge. It looks for lingering there. It looks for the same behavior on a rooftop. It alerts security guards. It alerts station staff. In some cases it gives loudspeaker warnings. Kyodo reported on 1 June 2026 that about 40 stations and commercial buildings in Japan had introduced the system. It reported that Asilla described two interventions, both undated. In the first the system detected a man loitering in a non-customer area of a commercial facility. A guard found him. He later said that he had intended to kill himself by jumping. In another, a child lingering near an upper-floor railing was found to have been writing a suicide note. Asilla does not say which version was used in these two interventions. All details come from the company via Kyodo. No confirmation from an operator is among the sources. None comes from the police. None comes from an academic. In July 2026 researchers at Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm reported on an AI camera system installed in late 2021. Suicide-related incidents on the tracks fell at 14 metro stations with it, compared with 86 other stations. They studied a different system and did not test Asilla's.

fields.summary: Asilla says that its behavior-analysis AI for security cameras alerted guards, who reached two people at apparent risk of suicide. The facilities are undisclosed. The dates are undisclosed.
fields.account: Tokyo-based Asilla's system assesses the likelihood that a person will jump by analyzing behavior on security-camera footage. Asilla says that it has trained the system since 2022 with around 200 facilities on about seven million pieces of footage. In a product release of 26 January 2024, Asilla describes a function in AI Security asilla version 2.4 that detects the risk of a jump. It uses the trajectories of movement. It uses position. It uses patterns of body motion. The system looks for pacing near a platform edge. It looks for lingering there. It looks for the same behavior on a rooftop. It alerts security guards. It alerts station staff. In some cases it gives loudspeaker warnings. Kyodo reported on 1 June 2026 that about 40 stations and commercial buildings in Japan had introduced the system. It reported that Asilla described two interventions, both undated. In the first the system detected a man loitering in a non-customer area of a commercial facility. A guard found him. He later said that he had intended to kill himself by jumping. In another, a child lingering near an upper-floor railing was found to have been writing a suicide note. Asilla does not say which version was used in these two interventions. All details come from the company via Kyodo. No confirmation from an operator is among the sources. None comes from the police. None comes from an academic. In July 2026 researchers at Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm reported on an AI camera system installed in late 2021. Suicide-related incidents on the tracks fell at 14 metro stations with it, compared with 86 other stations. They studied a different system and did not test Asilla's.

record.title: A man pleads guilty to stalking after OpenAI refers his threats to the FBI, which passes them to local police
record.summary: Through the FBI, OpenAI disclosed threats that a man wrote in ChatGPT against his ex-girlfriend. He later pleaded guilty to stalking.
record.account: A man wrote threats against his ex-girlfriend in ChatGPT. Court reporting describes an OpenAI emergency disclosure that reached the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office through the FBI. According to the probable cause affidavit cited by the Sun Sentinel, the FBI told the sheriff's office about the messages six days before the arrest. Deputies compared those messages with anonymous threats that the ex-girlfriend had preserved. The woman told detectives that she had not reported the man to police because she did not want to cause his behavior to escalate. The sheriff’s booking entry lists 29 May 2026 as his arrest date. BocaNewsNow reports that he pleaded guilty on 13 August 2026 to written threats. He pleaded guilty to aggravated stalking. He pleaded guilty to unlawful use of a two-way communication device. Adjudication was withheld. He received eight years of probation, two years of GPS monitoring. The court restricted his contact. It restricted his access to weapons. Reporters cite court documents. They do not reproduce the complete affidavit. They do not reproduce the plea order. Their reports support a police intervention and court restrictions. The sources do not show that an attack would otherwise have occurred.

display.answer: The Sun Sentinel report of 14 August 2026 draws on the sheriff's office probable cause affidavit and the State Attorney's Office. The BocaNewsNow report of 27 August 2026 draws on court records. The booking entry of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office shows the arrest date. OpenAI describes its general review policy in a post. No source reproduces the complete affidavit, the complete chats, the disclosure or the plea order.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: Through the FBI, OpenAI disclosed threats that a man wrote in ChatGPT against his ex-girlfriend. He later pleaded guilty to stalking.
fields.account: A man wrote threats against his ex-girlfriend in ChatGPT. Court reporting describes an OpenAI emergency disclosure that reached the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office through the FBI. According to the probable cause affidavit cited by the Sun Sentinel, the FBI told the sheriff's office about the messages six days before the arrest. Deputies compared those messages with anonymous threats that the ex-girlfriend had preserved. The woman told detectives that she had not reported the man to police because she did not want to cause his behavior to escalate. The sheriff’s booking entry lists 29 May 2026 as his arrest date. BocaNewsNow reports that he pleaded guilty on 13 August 2026 to written threats. He pleaded guilty to aggravated stalking. He pleaded guilty to unlawful use of a two-way communication device. Adjudication was withheld. He received eight years of probation, two years of GPS monitoring. The court restricted his contact. It restricted his access to weapons. Reporters cite court documents. They do not reproduce the complete affidavit. They do not reproduce the plea order. Their reports support a police intervention and court restrictions. The sources do not show that an attack would otherwise have occurred.

details.label: Focus
details.value: Public safety

details.label: Purpose
details.value: The Frankfurt police use the AI in the Bahnhofsviertel's Videoschutzanlage to identify people remotely, in real time, from their biometric features. The Hessian police law, amended in February 2025, allows this for narrow purposes such as finding missing persons. In their press release, the police called this case the system's first genuine positive hit.

details.label: Contribution of the AI
details.value: In their press release, the police describe the system's contribution step by step. After an emergency order that a judge confirmed, the girl's photo was entered into the database. Late on 9 October the AI produced an automated match alert for Taunusstraße. A video operator checked it, and a patrol confirmed it in person. The police had only indications that she might be in the district, so the AI supplied the place and the moment. Human verification and the patrol did the rest. Whether and how soon conventional patrols would have found her is not reported.

record.title: Frankfurt police find a missing 16-year-old in crisis on Taunusstraße within a day of her disappearance, after a judge-confirmed emergency order let the Bahnhofsviertel camera system's AI search for her face
record.summary: Frankfurt police found a missing 16-year-old in crisis within a day. The face recognition software VAS Videmo360 had flagged her on a Bahnhofsviertel camera, under an order that a judge confirmed.
record.account: On 8 October 2025 a 16-year-old was reported missing after failing to return to the psychiatric facility in Hesse where she lived. A farewell letter pointed to an acute psychological crisis. Indications placed her in Frankfurt's Bahnhofsviertel. Citing imminent danger, Frankfurt's police president issued an emergency order, which a judge confirmed. The order let the police enter her photograph into the AI-assisted camera system that had run in the district since July 2025. The system operates under the Hessian police law amended in February 2025. Late on 9 October the system showed a match on Taunusstraße. A video operator checked it. A patrol confirmed it. Officers took the girl into protective custody. They returned her to the child and adolescent psychiatric facility. On 16 October 2025 the police announced the rescue. They called it the system's first genuine positive hit. In December 2025 the Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte (GFF) and Doña Carmen sued at the Frankfurt Administrative Court. They asked the court to refer the sections of the police law that allow remote identification to the Federal Constitutional Court. In April 2026 netzpolitik.org reported that police had searched for a low double-digit number of persons with the system since July 2025. This was the only success. By then the Hessian Greens had also asked the Staatsgerichtshof to review the amendment to the police law behind real-time face recognition. In their filing of 22 April 2026 the plaintiffs argue that the law sets no danger threshold for searches for missing persons. In the filing, the plaintiffs cite the police's data protection impact assessment, in which the software is named as VAS Videmo360. By April 2026 the GFF reported that the police had extended the system to two more places in the city center. The system kept running, with an evaluation phase due from July 2026.
record.purpose: The Frankfurt police use the AI in the Bahnhofsviertel's Videoschutzanlage to identify people remotely, in real time, from their biometric features. The Hessian police law, amended in February 2025, allows this for narrow purposes such as finding missing persons. In their press release, the police called this case the system's first genuine positive hit.
record.system: AI-assisted video analysis with real-time biometric remote identification in the Frankfurt Bahnhofsviertel police video surveillance system (Videoschutzanlage), monitored from the police Video-Operation-Center
record.model_version: VAS Videmo360 video analysis system (product named in the police data protection impact assessment, as cited in the GFF filing); the police say that only the vendor knows the exact specifications of the face-template model
record.deployer: Polizeipräsidium Frankfurt am Main (Hessian police)

ratings.reason: A 16-year-old whose farewell letter led police to assume an acute psychological crisis was located in the Bahnhofsviertel within a day. She was returned to psychiatric care. The police describe this as averting danger to life and limb. But the police have not said what would otherwise have happened, so their account does not show that a life was saved.

The Frankfurt police recorded the first confirmed success of a system in use since July 2025. The police president and the interior minister cited it as validation. netzpolitik.org reported in April 2026 that it was still the only success among a low double-digit number of searches. The operational gain is modest.

ai_role.statement: In their press release, the police describe the system's contribution step by step. After an emergency order that a judge confirmed, the girl's photo was entered into the database. Late on 9 October the AI produced an automated match alert for Taunusstraße. A video operator checked it, and a patrol confirmed it in person. The police had only indications that she might be in the district, so the AI supplied the place and the moment. Human verification and the patrol did the rest. Whether and how soon conventional patrols would have found her is not reported.

evidence.citation: Polizeipräsidium Frankfurt am Main, reproduced by Heßberger K (2025). Künstliche Intelligenz lokalisiert 16-jährige Vermisste im Frankfurter Bahnhofsviertel. evidence.title: Künstliche Intelligenz lokalisiert 16-jährige Vermisste im Frankfurter Bahnhofsviertel

evidence.quote_translation: As early as October 9, just one day after the missing-person report, an automated hit notification for the area of Taunusstraße was displayed in the late evening hours in the Video-Operation-Center of the Frankfurt police.

evidence.quote_translation: Artificial intelligence locates missing 16-year-old in the Bahnhofsviertel - girl taken into care by police officers

evidence.citation: Euler R (2025). Polizei Frankfurt findet vermisstes Mädchen mithilfe von KI. Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, 16 October 2025, 15:42, paywalled beyond the opening paragraphs.
evidence.title: Polizei Frankfurt findet vermisstes Mädchen mithilfe von KI
evidence.quote: Mithilfe künstlicher Intelligenz hat die Polizei in der vergangenen Woche eine vermisste Sechzehnjährige im Frankfurter Bahnhofsviertel lokalisiert und in Obhut genommen.
evidence.quote_translation: With the help of artificial intelligence, the police last week located a missing sixteen-year-old girl in Frankfurt's Bahnhofsviertel and took her into care.

evidence.citation: Pfeiffer-Goldmann D (2025). KI-Einsatz in Frankfurt erstmals erfolgreich – vermisstes Mädchen wiedergefunden. Frankfurter Neue Presse, 17 October 2025, 14:10. Quotes police spokesman Patrick Rüter and Interior Minister Roman Poseck.
evidence.title: KI-Einsatz in Frankfurt erstmals erfolgreich – vermisstes Mädchen wiedergefunden
evidence.quote: Einen Tag später habe die KI automatisch einen Treffer in der Taunusstraße gemeldet. Ein Videooperator habe das überprüft
evidence.quote_translation: One day later, the AI had automatically reported a hit on Taunusstraße. A video operator had checked it

evidence.citation: Schröder D (2025). KI rettet vermisstes Mädchen (16) aus Drogen-Sumpf von Frankfurt. Bild, 17 October 2025. The quoted sentence is attributed to Police President Stefan Müller.
evidence.title: KI rettet vermisstes Mädchen (16) aus Drogen-Sumpf von Frankfurt
evidence.quote: Der erste echte positive Treffer zeigt eindrucksvoll, wie uns auf Basis des neuen Polizeigesetzes modernste Technik zuverlässig und erfolgreich bei der Abwehr von Gefahren für Leib und Leben hilft.
evidence.quote_translation: The first true positive hit shows impressively how, on the basis of the new police law, state-of-the-art technology reliably and successfully helps us avert dangers to life and limb.

evidence.citation: Schwarzbeck M (2026). Rotlichtviertel Frankfurt am Main: Hier analysiert die Polizei jedes Gesicht. netzpolitik.org, 22 April 2026. Schwarzbeck reports 29 cameras in the Bahnhofsviertel, 19 of them usable for automated face recognition. Schwarzbeck also reports a low double-digit number of persons searched since July 2025 and this case as the only success.
evidence.title: Rotlichtviertel Frankfurt am Main: Hier analysiert die Polizei jedes Gesicht
evidence.quote: Erfolg gab es nur einmal, als eine vermisste 16-Jährige mit der Kamera-KI identifiziert wurde
evidence.quote_translation: There was success only once, when a missing 16-year-old was identified with the camera AI

evidence.citation: Kissel L, Pfeuffer-Rooschüz L (2026). Hessen erfand den Datenschutz – und ist heute Vorreiter bei Videoüberwachung mit KI. hessenschau.de, 25 March 2026. The authors cite this case as the pilot's one reported success and include criticism from the Chaos Computer Club and the Hessian commissioner for data protection.
evidence.title: Hessen erfand den Datenschutz – und ist heute Vorreiter bei Videoüberwachung mit KI
evidence.quote: Diese Anlagen können von einem Hilfsmittel zu einem Herrschaftsmittel werden
evidence.quote_translation: These systems can turn from an aid into an instrument of domination

evidence.citation: Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte, Doña Carmen e. V. and Prigge, J. (2026). Klagebegründung an das Verwaltungsgericht Frankfurt am Main, 22 April 2026. The plaintiffs oppose the system and wrote this filing. They report what the police said in their reply of 17 December 2025 and in their data protection impact assessment. They argue that the law allows searches for missing persons without a set danger threshold.
evidence.title: Klagebegründung an das Verwaltungsgericht Frankfurt am Main
evidence.quote: Einzig normierte Voraussetzung ist, dass eine Person im Datenbestand der polizeilichen Auskunfts- und Fahndungssysteme als vermisst gespeichert ist und die Suche nach dieser Person auf diese Weise unbedingt erforderlich ist.
evidence.quote_translation: The only statutory precondition is that a person is stored as missing in the database of the police information and wanted-persons systems and that searching for this person in this way is absolutely necessary.

evidence.citation: Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte (2026). Large-scale AI-supported video surveillance in Frankfurt city center. GFF case page. The sentence on the extension appears in the Internet Archive copy of 22 April 2026. The civil-rights group is a plaintiff against the system. The group states on the page when the suit was filed and that the police extended the system.
evidence.title: Large-scale AI-supported video surveillance in Frankfurt city center
evidence.quote: The police have now expanded the use of this AI system to two additional locations in the city center-and it is expected that more locations will follow.

produced_by: A missing-person report with concrete signs of danger to life (a farewell letter) and indications of the person's whereabouts inside the camera-covered district
A legal basis, the Hessian police law amended in February 2025, plus a police-president emergency order confirmed by a judge. These let the girl's photo be entered into the system
An AI-assisted camera network already running in the Bahnhofsviertel since July 2025, with a staffed Video-Operation-Center. Patrols close enough to verify and act on a match the same evening
must_hold: The person passes in front of cameras suitable for automated recognition. netzpolitik.org counted 19 such cameras among the district's 29
A human operator and a patrol verify the automated match before anyone is taken into custody
The search stays within the narrow legal purposes the law allows, which Bild lists as missing persons, kidnapping victims and victims of human trafficking

later.note: By April 2026 the Hessian Greens had asked the Staatsgerichtshof to review the amendment to the police law behind real-time face recognition. Juanita Henning of Doña Carmen had sued with the GFF at the Frankfurt administrative court and asked for a referral to the Federal Constitutional Court. The system kept running, with an evaluation phase due from July 2026.
later.quote: Die lassen mit einem Normenkontrollantrag beim Staatsgerichtshof klären , ob die der Echtzeit-Fernidentifizierung zugrunde liegende Polizeigesetzänderung rechtens war. Eine Überprüfung der Rechtsgrundlage streben auch Juanita Henning und die GFF an. data.retained_case_account: On 8 October 2025 a 16-year-old was reported missing after failing to return to the psychiatric facility in Hesse where she lived. A farewell letter pointed to an acute psychological crisis. Indications placed her in Frankfurt's Bahnhofsviertel. Citing imminent danger, Frankfurt's police president issued an emergency order, confirmed by a judge. So her photograph could be entered into the AI-assisted camera system running in the district since July 2025. It operates under the Hessian police law amended in February 2025. Late on 9 October the system flagged a match on Taunusstraße. A video operator checked it and a patrol confirmed it. Officers took the girl into protective custody and returned her to the child and adolescent psychiatric facility.

fields.account: On 8 October 2025 a 16-year-old was reported missing after failing to return to the psychiatric facility in Hesse where she lived. A farewell letter pointed to an acute psychological crisis. Indications placed her in Frankfurt's Bahnhofsviertel. Citing imminent danger, Frankfurt's police president issued an emergency order, which a judge confirmed. The order let the police enter her photograph into the AI-assisted camera system that had run in the district since July 2025. The system operates under the Hessian police law amended in February 2025. Late on 9 October the system showed a match on Taunusstraße. A video operator checked it. A patrol confirmed it. Officers took the girl into protective custody. They returned her to the child and adolescent psychiatric facility. On 16 October 2025 the police announced the rescue. They called it the system's first genuine positive hit. In December 2025 the Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte (GFF) and Doña Carmen sued at the Frankfurt Administrative Court. They asked the court to refer the sections of the police law that allow remote identification to the Federal Constitutional Court. In April 2026 netzpolitik.org reported that police had searched for a low double-digit number of persons with the system since July 2025. This was the only success. By then the Hessian Greens had also asked the Staatsgerichtshof to review the amendment to the police law behind real-time face recognition. In their filing of 22 April 2026 the plaintiffs argue that the law sets no danger threshold for searches for missing persons. In the filing, the plaintiffs cite the police's data protection impact assessment, in which the software is named as VAS Videmo360. By April 2026 the GFF reported that the police had extended the system to two more places in the city center. The system kept running, with an evaluation phase due from July 2026.

display.answer: The account of the search comes from the Frankfurt police's press release of 16 October 2025, which Rhein Main Verlag reproduced and the newspapers covered. The software name comes from the police's data protection impact assessment, as cited in the plaintiffs' court filing of 22 April 2026. Reports by netzpolitik.org and hessenschau.de cover the system's later record and its critics.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: Frankfurt police found a missing 16-year-old in crisis within a day. The face recognition software VAS Videmo360 had flagged her on a Bahnhofsviertel camera, under an order that a judge confirmed.
fields.account: On 8 October 2025 a 16-year-old was reported missing after failing to return to the psychiatric facility in Hesse where she lived. A farewell letter pointed to an acute psychological crisis. Indications placed her in Frankfurt's Bahnhofsviertel. Citing imminent danger, Frankfurt's police president issued an emergency order, which a judge confirmed. The order let the police enter her photograph into the AI-assisted camera system that had run in the district since July 2025. The system operates under the Hessian police law amended in February 2025. Late on 9 October the system showed a match on Taunusstraße. A video operator checked it. A patrol confirmed it. Officers took the girl into protective custody. They returned her to the child and adolescent psychiatric facility. On 16 October 2025 the police announced the rescue. They called it the system's first genuine positive hit. In December 2025 the Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte (GFF) and Doña Carmen sued at the Frankfurt Administrative Court. They asked the court to refer the sections of the police law that allow remote identification to the Federal Constitutional Court. In April 2026 netzpolitik.org reported that police had searched for a low double-digit number of persons with the system since July 2025. This was the only success. By then the Hessian Greens had also asked the Staatsgerichtshof to review the amendment to the police law behind real-time face recognition. In their filing of 22 April 2026 the plaintiffs argue that the law sets no danger threshold for searches for missing persons. In the filing, the plaintiffs cite the police's data protection impact assessment, in which the software is named as VAS Videmo360. By April 2026 the GFF reported that the police had extended the system to two more places in the city center. The system kept running, with an evaluation phase due from July 2026.

record.title: UNEP records eight methane mitigations in Turkmenistan after MARS notifications
record.summary: UNEP lists eight methane leaks in Turkmenistan that were mitigated from November 2024 to March 2026 after alerts from its Methane Alert and Response System (MARS), which uses AI.
record.account: UNEP states that its Methane Alert and Response System (MARS) combines satellite observations, scientific review and AI to identify emissions for action by governments. Companies are meant to act on them. In its MARS index of mitigations, UNEP lists eight cases in Turkmenistan: two in Yelguyi in November 2024, one in Babarap in June 2025, one in Gugurtli field in July 2025, one in Balguyy in August 2025, two in Dauletabad in February 2026 and one in Lebap Province in March 2026. Each entry has a source identifier with a link to an individual case document. UNEP describes these as mitigations that MARS helped prompt. It says that MARS helped verify them. In its document for case TKM_S_406, updated on 15 April 2026, UNEP states that MARS first detected the Lebap pipeline leak on 22 June 2025. It states that MARS gave an estimate of 16,000 tonnes of methane from 47 plumes. UNEP reports that the operator repaired a corroded flowline. It reports that satellites detected no further emissions after 7 March 2026. The Guardian reported on 31 August 2026 that the first Turkmen leak had been fixed in November 2024. It reported that Turkmenistan had stopped eight leaks by repairing corroded pipes, faulty wells and failing flares. The MARS program manager told the Guardian that Turkmenistan's response rate was growing month by month. The manager added that eight cases did not yet change the size of Turkmenistan's emissions as a whole. UNEP has not isolated the contribution of AI from that of analysts, notifications and physical repairs. It has not quantified their combined benefit.

fields.account: UNEP states that its Methane Alert and Response System (MARS) combines satellite observations, scientific review and AI to identify emissions for action by governments. Companies are meant to act on them. In its MARS index of mitigations, UNEP lists eight cases in Turkmenistan: two in Yelguyi in November 2024, one in Babarap in June 2025, one in Gugurtli field in July 2025, one in Balguyy in August 2025, two in Dauletabad in February 2026 and one in Lebap Province in March 2026. Each entry has a source identifier with a link to an individual case document. UNEP describes these as mitigations that MARS helped prompt. It says that MARS helped verify them. In its document for case TKM_S_406, updated on 15 April 2026, UNEP states that MARS first detected the Lebap pipeline leak on 22 June 2025. It states that MARS gave an estimate of 16,000 tonnes of methane from 47 plumes. UNEP reports that the operator repaired a corroded flowline. It reports that satellites detected no further emissions after 7 March 2026. The Guardian reported on 31 August 2026 that the first Turkmen leak had been fixed in November 2024. It reported that Turkmenistan had stopped eight leaks by repairing corroded pipes, faulty wells and failing flares. The MARS program manager told the Guardian that Turkmenistan's response rate was growing month by month. The manager added that eight cases did not yet change the size of Turkmenistan's emissions as a whole. UNEP has not isolated the contribution of AI from that of analysts, notifications and physical repairs. It has not quantified their combined benefit.

record.title: Chilean prosecutors credit the AI model “Fiscal Heredia” with identifying a 10-member gang. A court accredits 8 “encerrona” robberies
record.summary: In Operación Influencer (11 May 2023) the authorities detained a gang of 10 aged 15–22 behind eight accredited violent robberies. Prosecutors credit the AI model Fiscal Heredia.
record.account: In the early hours of Thursday 11 May 2023, Focos Occidente and the Brigada de Investigación Criminal of Chile's Policía de Investigaciones carried out a joint investigation. They executed 30 search warrants across Maipú, Pudahuel, Cerro Navia and other comunas. There were 17 detentions. Ten of them were linked to “encerronas” (robbery with intimidation or violence) whose perpetrators posted their robberies on TikTok. On 12 May 2023 the television channel T13 quoted Fiscal Nacional Ángel Valencia saying that the algorithm accelerates criminal analysis. T13 reports that after three members were arrested, the model searched their links. It reports that the model raised persons of interest whom victims later identified. The Fiscalía de Chile issued a regional news release on 17 May 2023. It says that the ten were identified through the software Fiscal Heredia (Herramienta para el Estudio del Delito Usando Inteligencia Artificial). The Fiscalía describes it as an AI model that several universities developed. The Ministerio Público adopted it in March 2023. The model proposes probable participants from the records of the prosecution. It draws on police records. Prosecutors and police then work them up. The Noveno Juzgado de Garantía accredited the eight robberies. Four adults went to preventive detention. Four adolescents remained in provisional internment. On 25 August 2026 the Fiscalía named the developers as the Universidad de Chile, the Universidad del Biobío and the Universidad de los Andes. They worked with the Ministerio Público in a project, funded by the Fondo de Fomento al Desarrollo Científico y Tecnológico (Fondef), that began in 2020. The Fiscalía reported that the tool, now called Fiscal HeredIA, runs in 15 regional prosecutor's offices with more than 1,000 prosecutors and other users. It reported that the tool won second place in the IFORS Prize for OR in Development 2026.

data.retained_case_account: The Fiscalía de Chile's regional news release describes a joint investigation by Focos Occidente and the PDI's Brigada de Investigación Criminal. In the early hours of Thursday 11 May 2023 it led to 30 search warrants across Maipú, Pudahuel, Cerro Navia and other comunas. There were 17 detentions, ten linked to “encerronas” (robbery with intimidation or violence) whose perpetrators posted their robberies on TikTok. The release says they were identified through the software Fiscal Heredia (Herramienta para el Estudio del Delito Usando Inteligencia Artificial). It is an AI model developed by several universities and incorporated into the Ministerio Público in March 2023. It proposes probable participants from prosecution and police records for prosecutors and police to work up. The Noveno Juzgado de Garantía accredited the eight robberies. Four adults went to preventive detention and four adolescents remained in provisional internment. T13 quotes Fiscal Nacional Ángel Valencia saying the algorithm accelerates criminal analysis. It reports that after three members were arrested the AI searched their links to raise persons of interest later identified by victims.

fields.account: In the early hours of Thursday 11 May 2023, Focos Occidente and the Brigada de Investigación Criminal of Chile's Policía de Investigaciones carried out a joint investigation. They executed 30 search warrants across Maipú, Pudahuel, Cerro Navia and other comunas. There were 17 detentions. Ten of them were linked to “encerronas” (robbery with intimidation or violence) whose perpetrators posted their robberies on TikTok. On 12 May 2023 the television channel T13 quoted Fiscal Nacional Ángel Valencia saying that the algorithm accelerates criminal analysis. T13 reports that after three members were arrested, the model searched their links. It reports that the model raised persons of interest whom victims later identified. The Fiscalía de Chile issued a regional news release on 17 May 2023. It says that the ten were identified through the software Fiscal Heredia (Herramienta para el Estudio del Delito Usando Inteligencia Artificial). The Fiscalía describes it as an AI model that several universities developed. The Ministerio Público adopted it in March 2023. The model proposes probable participants from the records of the prosecution. It draws on police records. Prosecutors and police then work them up. The Noveno Juzgado de Garantía accredited the eight robberies. Four adults went to preventive detention. Four adolescents remained in provisional internment. On 25 August 2026 the Fiscalía named the developers as the Universidad de Chile, the Universidad del Biobío and the Universidad de los Andes. They worked with the Ministerio Público in a project, funded by the Fondo de Fomento al Desarrollo Científico y Tecnológico (Fondef), that began in 2020. The Fiscalía reported that the tool, now called Fiscal HeredIA, runs in 15 regional prosecutor's offices with more than 1,000 prosecutors and other users. It reported that the tool won second place in the IFORS Prize for OR in Development 2026.

record.title: INEC's Automated Biometric Identification System invalidates 2,780,756 ineligible voter registrations (22.6%) before Nigeria's 2023 election
record.summary: Nigeria's electoral commission reported on 26 October 2022 that its Automated Biometric Identification System (ABIS) flagged 2,780,756 (22.6%) of 2021–22 registrations as ineligible.
record.account: On 12 September 2022 Festus Okoye, a commissioner of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), gave early figures. He said that 1,126,359 of 2,523,458 registrants (28 June 2021 to 14 January 2022) were delisted after they were found invalid. Punch reported that ABIS processing of later registrations was ongoing. This benefit is dated to 26 October 2022, when INEC's chairman, Professor Mahmood Yakubu, addressed political parties in Abuja. The Nigerian Democratic Report reproduced the address. He said that the Continuous Voter Registration data (28 June 2021 to 31 July 2022) was cleaned with the Automated Biometric Identification System (ABIS). In this cleaning, 2,780,756 registrations (22.6%) were identified as ineligible and invalidated. Among them were double registrants. Multiple registrants were among them. The count included underage persons. It covered fake registrations that failed INEC's business rules. That left 9,518,188 valid registrations after ABIS cleaning. INEC identified 23 registration officers for sanctions. On 20 January 2023 BusinessDay argued that some fake registrants evaded ABIS. It argued that underage registrants evaded ABIS. In its view, rates of invalidation were regionally lopsided. The European Union Election Observation Mission reported on 27 June 2023 that more than 2.8 million registrations were removed. Some were double. Others were for underage people. Fake registrations formed a third group. The mission called this a positive development. It reported that stakeholders widely acknowledged that underage registrants remained, in unknown numbers. By its account, the register has never been audited. The mission recommended an external independent audit of the voter register. The vendor of ABIS has not been named.

fields.summary: Nigeria's electoral commission reported on 26 October 2022 that its Automated Biometric Identification System (ABIS) flagged 2,780,756 (22.6%) of 2021–22 registrations as ineligible.
fields.account: On 12 September 2022 Festus Okoye, a commissioner of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), gave early figures. He said that 1,126,359 of 2,523,458 registrants (28 June 2021 to 14 January 2022) were delisted after they were found invalid. Punch reported that ABIS processing of later registrations was ongoing. This benefit is dated to 26 October 2022, when INEC's chairman, Professor Mahmood Yakubu, addressed political parties in Abuja. The Nigerian Democratic Report reproduced the address. He said that the Continuous Voter Registration data (28 June 2021 to 31 July 2022) was cleaned with the Automated Biometric Identification System (ABIS). In this cleaning, 2,780,756 registrations (22.6%) were identified as ineligible and invalidated. Among them were double registrants. Multiple registrants were among them. The count included underage persons. It covered fake registrations that failed INEC's business rules. That left 9,518,188 valid registrations after ABIS cleaning. INEC identified 23 registration officers for sanctions. On 20 January 2023 BusinessDay argued that some fake registrants evaded ABIS. It argued that underage registrants evaded ABIS. In its view, rates of invalidation were regionally lopsided. The European Union Election Observation Mission reported on 27 June 2023 that more than 2.8 million registrations were removed. Some were double. Others were for underage people. Fake registrations formed a third group. The mission called this a positive development. It reported that stakeholders widely acknowledged that underage registrants remained, in unknown numbers. By its account, the register has never been audited. The mission recommended an external independent audit of the voter register. The vendor of ABIS has not been named.

record.title: Darpan, a Telangana State Police tool, matches a boy missing from Allahabad to a child home in Assam, where his parents identify him after five years
record.summary: Darpan, a Telangana State Police facial-recognition tool, matched a boy missing from Allahabad since 14 July 2015 to a boy in a child home in Goalpara, Assam, where his parents identified him.
record.account: A boy went missing from his home in Allahabad (Uttar Pradesh) on 14 July 2015, aged eight. ETV Bharat describes him as a resident of Handia in Allahabad. The investigation lay with Handia police station. On 23 July 2015, Goalpara police found him. They took him to a child welfare center at Goalpara, Assam (spelled “Golapara” in the reports). Telangana State Police built Darpan, a tool for recognizing faces. It matches photographs of missing children against photographs of children lodged in child homes across the country. In a routine run, Darpan matched his photograph to the record of a missing child from Uttar Pradesh. Telangana Police notified Handia police. His parents traveled to Goalpara. They identified him. Swati Lakra, Additional Director General of Police (ADGP) of the Telangana Police Women Safety Wing, announced the reunion on 9 October 2020. The exact day of the reunion is not known. ANI reported on 12 October 2020 that Lakra had told it that Telangana State Police built Darpan in 2018. She said that the police draw data from child care institutions. They take data from the central Track the Missing Child portal. The Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and System (CCTNS) gives them data. According to her, Darpan had helped reunite about 33 children by then. In July 2023, Deccan Chronicle reported that Hyderabad police were still using Darpan. The paper reported that Darpan had helped reunite 36 children.

record.title: Odakyu Electric Railway's Panasonic deep-learning “fall detection system” flags a staggering passenger days after it starts on existing cameras at Kyōdō and Soshigaya-Ōkura stations
record.summary: Panasonic's fall detection system at Odakyu alerts staff to people on the tracks. It does the same at the platform edge. The vendor reports that it flagged a staggering passenger on 3 April 2020.
record.account: Pre-learning ran at Kyōdō (経堂) and Soshigaya-Ōkura (祖師ヶ谷大蔵) stations on the Odakyu Line from December 2019. In pre-learning, each camera's detection area was set. The system was taught to distinguish people from trains. On 30 March 2020 Odakyu Electric Railway announced a 転落検知システム (fall detection system) in a press release that Nikkei republished. Impress Watch reported the launch on 31 March 2020. The system would operate from the first train on 1 April 2020 at both stations, using video from existing station cameras. It was built with Panasonic System Solutions Japan. It applies Panasonic's image-analysis technology to the camera feeds in real time, together with Panasonic's deep-learning technology. It alerts a dedicated terminal in the station office, showing the camera image, when it detects a person fallen from the platform onto the tracks. It does the same for a person who has stayed at the platform edge for a set time. Such a person risks contact with a train. Staff can then take safety measures such as an emergency stop. At the launch, Odakyu and Impress Watch reported no detection, no prevented accident and no performance figure. In a case study of September 2020, Panasonic Connect reports a detection on 3 April 2020. The system detected a passenger staggering at the platform edge at Kyōdō. Staff took safety measures. Panasonic says that this prevented an accident. The same case study reports misdetections caused by sunlight. Impress Watch reported on 7 October 2024 a separate trial of Asilla's behavior-recognition “AI Security asilla” on all 20 existing cameras at Kakio and Tamagawa-Gakuen-mae stations. It ran from 10 October 2024 to 9 January 2025. It tested detection of falls from the platform, wheelchair users, white-cane users, people lingering on the platform, disputes between passengers and suspicious objects. Results were not reported. In its safety reports, Odakyu lists the system as operating at both stations through July 2025. In its report of July 2026, it no longer lists the system. The report shows platform doors installed at Soshigaya-Ōkura, with doors scheduled for Kyōdō in fiscal 2026.

data.retained_case_account: Odakyu Electric Railway announced on 30 March 2020 (press release republished by Nikkei) a 転落検知システム (fall detection system). It would operate from the first train on 1 April 2020 at Kyōdō (経堂) and Soshigaya-Ōkura (祖師ヶ谷大蔵) stations on the Odakyu Line. It uses video from existing station cameras. Built with Panasonic System Solutions Japan, the system applies Panasonic's image-analysis and deep-learning technology to analyze the camera feeds in real time. It alerts a dedicated terminal in the station office, showing the camera image, when it detects a person fallen from the platform onto the tracks. It does the same for a person who has stayed at the platform edge for a set time and risks contact with a train. Staff can then take safety measures such as an emergency stop. Pre-learning to set each camera's detection area and to distinguish people from trains had run at both stations since December 2019. Impress Watch reported the launch on 31 March 2020. Neither source reports any detection, prevented accident or performance figure, and no later outcome report was found. Impress Watch (7 October 2024) reported a separate trial of Asilla's behavior-recognition “AI Security asilla” on all 20 existing cameras at Kakio and Tamagawa-Gakuen-mae stations. It ran from 10 October 2024 to 9 January 2025. It tested detection of falls from the platform, wheelchair and white-cane users, people lingering on the platform, disputes between passengers and suspicious objects. Results were not reported. Romanizations of station names are ours; the sources give them in Japanese.

fields.account: Pre-learning ran at Kyōdō (経堂) and Soshigaya-Ōkura (祖師ヶ谷大蔵) stations on the Odakyu Line from December 2019. In pre-learning, each camera's detection area was set. The system was taught to distinguish people from trains. On 30 March 2020 Odakyu Electric Railway announced a 転落検知システム (fall detection system) in a press release that Nikkei republished. Impress Watch reported the launch on 31 March 2020. The system would operate from the first train on 1 April 2020 at both stations, using video from existing station cameras. It was built with Panasonic System Solutions Japan. It applies Panasonic's image-analysis technology to the camera feeds in real time, together with Panasonic's deep-learning technology. It alerts a dedicated terminal in the station office, showing the camera image, when it detects a person fallen from the platform onto the tracks. It does the same for a person who has stayed at the platform edge for a set time. Such a person risks contact with a train. Staff can then take safety measures such as an emergency stop. At the launch, Odakyu and Impress Watch reported no detection, no prevented accident and no performance figure. In a case study of September 2020, Panasonic Connect reports a detection on 3 April 2020. The system detected a passenger staggering at the platform edge at Kyōdō. Staff took safety measures. Panasonic says that this prevented an accident. The same case study reports misdetections caused by sunlight. Impress Watch reported on 7 October 2024 a separate trial of Asilla's behavior-recognition “AI Security asilla” on all 20 existing cameras at Kakio and Tamagawa-Gakuen-mae stations. It ran from 10 October 2024 to 9 January 2025. It tested detection of falls from the platform, wheelchair users, white-cane users, people lingering on the platform, disputes between passengers and suspicious objects. Results were not reported. In its safety reports, Odakyu lists the system as operating at both stations through July 2025. In its report of July 2026, it no longer lists the system. The report shows platform doors installed at Soshigaya-Ōkura, with doors scheduled for Kyōdō in fiscal 2026.

display.answer: Nikkei republished Odakyu's press release of 30 March 2020, and Impress Watch reported the same launch. The detection on 3 April 2020 comes only from Panasonic Connect's case study. The safety reports of 2025 and 2026 are Odakyu's own.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: Panasonic's fall detection system at Odakyu alerts staff to people on the tracks. It does the same at the platform edge. The vendor reports that it flagged a staggering passenger on 3 April 2020.
fields.account: Pre-learning ran at Kyōdō (経堂) and Soshigaya-Ōkura (祖師ヶ谷大蔵) stations on the Odakyu Line from December 2019. In pre-learning, each camera's detection area was set. The system was taught to distinguish people from trains. On 30 March 2020 Odakyu Electric Railway announced a 転落検知システム (fall detection system) in a press release that Nikkei republished. Impress Watch reported the launch on 31 March 2020. The system would operate from the first train on 1 April 2020 at both stations, using video from existing station cameras. It was built with Panasonic System Solutions Japan. It applies Panasonic's image-analysis technology to the camera feeds in real time, together with Panasonic's deep-learning technology. It alerts a dedicated terminal in the station office, showing the camera image, when it detects a person fallen from the platform onto the tracks. It does the same for a person who has stayed at the platform edge for a set time. Such a person risks contact with a train. Staff can then take safety measures such as an emergency stop. At the launch, Odakyu and Impress Watch reported no detection, no prevented accident and no performance figure. In a case study of September 2020, Panasonic Connect reports a detection on 3 April 2020. The system detected a passenger staggering at the platform edge at Kyōdō. Staff took safety measures. Panasonic says that this prevented an accident. The same case study reports misdetections caused by sunlight. Impress Watch reported on 7 October 2024 a separate trial of Asilla's behavior-recognition “AI Security asilla” on all 20 existing cameras at Kakio and Tamagawa-Gakuen-mae stations. It ran from 10 October 2024 to 9 January 2025. It tested detection of falls from the platform, wheelchair users, white-cane users, people lingering on the platform, disputes between passengers and suspicious objects. Results were not reported. In its safety reports, Odakyu lists the system as operating at both stations through July 2025. In its report of July 2026, it no longer lists the system. The report shows platform doors installed at Soshigaya-Ōkura, with doors scheduled for Kyōdō in fiscal 2026.

value.text: The software detected and alerted. Station staff could then confirm the situation and order an emergency stop.

details.value: The AI ranked blocks of 3 x 3 km by risk, and that ranking decided where patrols went. The rangers did not know the risk class of each block. Patrols found poaching in high-risk blocks and none in low-risk blocks. The authors caution that the increased findings in their first test in Queen Elizabeth National Park “may be partially explained by factors beyond the predictive model”. record.title: Rangers following patrol plans from PAWS remove over 1,000 snares in a month in Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary, Cambodia
record.summary: Rangers on patrols directed by PAWS in Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary removed over 1,000 snares in December 2018, versus 200–300 in a typical month.
record.account: PAWS (Protection Assistant for Wildlife Security) is a machine-learning pipeline that predicts the risk of poaching. It uses the predictions to plan patrols. It was field-tested with WWF Cambodia and Ministry of Environment rangers in Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary, Cambodia, from December 2018. Rangers received the coordinates of the centers of fifteen blocks of 3 x 3 km, chosen from the risk predictions of PAWS. They were not told the risk class of each block. In the first month, 72 rangers in teams of eight detected poaching in 32 cells. They removed over one thousand snares. They had reported removing two or three hundred in an average month. Low-risk blocks yielded no poaching. A second trial ran from February to March 2019. In that trial, high-risk blocks yielded 7 detections in 22 cells. Low-risk blocks yielded 0 detections in 34 cells. The developers wrote up both trials in a peer-reviewed paper published in 2020. Staff of the operating organizations were co-authors. On 5 November 2020, Mongabay reported that PAWS had been incorporated into the SMART conservation software, which rangers use in parks around the world. The outlet reported that Srepok rangers had reported finding 5 to 20 times more snares since they started using PAWS.
record.purpose: Its developers built PAWS to predict where poaching will happen and to plan patrol routes that find and remove as many snares as possible. Removing snares is the intended benefit.
