fields.summary: A Los Angeles police drone observed a sleeping man with a suspected gun on a bus. Officers then sent in the Boston Dynamics Spot robot as a barrier. The gun proved to be a BB gun.
fields.account: Just before 4 a.m. on 8 November 2023, a passenger on a Metro bus in Hollywood reported an armed man aboard. The bus was at Melrose and Western avenues. The driver pulled over. He evacuated the other passengers. Officers got no response from the man. A two-hour standoff followed (Los Angeles Times via Police1, 9 November 2023). In its quarterly report, the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) says that patrol officers tried to talk with the man for about 75 minutes. They then declared an armed barricade. They called the special weapons and tactics (SWAT) team. The LAPD sent in its Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped. The LAPD states that a drone observed the sleeping man before the quadruped entered. It states that the drone also observed the suspected gun. It adds that SWAT chose the quadruped because a tracked robot could not have climbed the bus steps. By the LAPD's account, the quadruped climbed the bus steps. It then formed a barrier between the man and the suspected firearm. The LAPD does not describe the robot removing the weapon. The man woke. He left the bus. He was taken into custody about 6:40 a.m. The weapon was a BB gun (Police1). Police1 attributes the initial observation to the quadruped’s camera. In an account of October 2024, International Business Times says that the robot removed the gun. Deputy Chief David Kowalski approves each use. The robot cost nearly $300,000 (NBC). By 1 January 2025 SWAT had deployed the robot at least seven times, Spectrum News reported.

record.title: After a model of U.S. Customs and Border Protection flags a car at San Ysidro, officers arrest two people with over 75 kg of narcotics (2023)
record.summary: A machine-learning model of U.S. Customs and Border Protection flagged a car's crossing history at San Ysidro in 2023. Officers found over 75 kilograms of narcotics. They arrested two people.
record.account: In 2023 a car driving north from Mexico approached the Port of Entry at San Ysidro. A machine-learning model of U.S. Customs and Border Protection detected a suspicious pattern in its crossing history. The model marked the car for review. The alert came in under 1.4 seconds. An officer referred the car to secondary inspection. Officers found over 75 kilograms of narcotics in the rear quarter panels. More was in the gas tank. They seized the drugs. They seized the vehicle. They arrested the driver. They arrested the passenger. Eric Hysen, chief information officer of the Department of Homeland Security, described the event in congressional testimony on 14 September 2023. In his testimony he says that the car crossed recently. He gives no date. He said that without the model an officer would have had no cause to inspect the car more closely than at a normal stop. He told Congress that referrals from these models had led to 240 seizures in 2023 by mid-September. On its page about artificial intelligence, last updated on 27 November 2023, the department describes the same seizure and the arrest of the driver. At the Axios AI+ Summit on 28 November 2023, Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas described a matching event. He said that the model of the Office of Field Operations flagged in 1.4 seconds a “truck” that held about 75 kilograms of narcotics. In its Artificial Intelligence Roadmap of March 2024, the department repeats the account as a referral for secondary review that yielded over 75 kilograms of drugs. The drug and the date of the seizure have not been reported.

data.retained_case_account: In 2023 a car driving north from Mexico approached the Point of Entry at San Ysidro. A U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) machine-learning model identified a suspicious pattern in its border-crossing history and flagged it for review. DHS chief information officer Eric Hysen described the event in congressional testimony on September 14, 2023. An alert generated in under 1.4 seconds prompted an officer to refer the car to secondary inspection. Officers found over 75 kilograms of narcotics in the rear quarter panels and gas tank, seized the drugs and vehicle, and arrested the driver and passenger. At the Axios AI+ Summit on 28 November 2023 Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas described a matching case. The Office of Field Operations model flagged a “truck” in 1.4 seconds that held about 75 kilograms of narcotics. DHS's 2024 AI Roadmap repeats it: a secondary-review flag yielding over 75 kg of drugs. No source names the drug or the seizure date.

Mayorkas said the anomaly was identified in 1.4 seconds. The discovery of the narcotics and the arrest were done by officers in secondary review. No source states whether the car would have been referred without the flag. The model's counterfactual contribution is thus asserted by DHS, not demonstrated. The Monitor entry also bundles Mayorkas's claim that AI age-progression imagery has recovered abducted children. That claim names no case, date, or child.

fields.account: In 2023 a car driving north from Mexico approached the Port of Entry at San Ysidro. A machine-learning model of U.S. Customs and Border Protection detected a suspicious pattern in its crossing history. The model marked the car for review. The alert came in under 1.4 seconds. An officer referred the car to secondary inspection. Officers found over 75 kilograms of narcotics in the rear quarter panels. More was in the gas tank. They seized the drugs. They seized the vehicle. They arrested the driver. They arrested the passenger. Eric Hysen, chief information officer of the Department of Homeland Security, described the event in congressional testimony on 14 September 2023. In his testimony he says that the car crossed recently. He gives no date. He said that without the model an officer would have had no cause to inspect the car more closely than at a normal stop. He told Congress that referrals from these models had led to 240 seizures in 2023 by mid-September. On its page about artificial intelligence, last updated on 27 November 2023, the department describes the same seizure and the arrest of the driver. At the Axios AI+ Summit on 28 November 2023, Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas described a matching event. He said that the model of the Office of Field Operations flagged in 1.4 seconds a “truck” that held about 75 kilograms of narcotics. In its Artificial Intelligence Roadmap of March 2024, the department repeats the account as a referral for secondary review that yielded over 75 kilograms of drugs. The drug and the date of the seizure have not been reported.

record.title: Cal Fire holds a fire near Mount Laguna to under a quarter acre after human operators verify smoke that ALERTCalifornia's AI flags at 3 am
record.summary: ALERTCalifornia's AI flagged smoke on a Cleveland National Forest camera at about 3 a.m. on 5 August 2023. Cal Fire held the verified fire under a quarter acre.
record.account: The ALERTCalifornia AI, a machine-learned model run by the University of California San Diego, scans live feeds from more than 1,000 cameras. It began scanning the feeds at the end of June 2023 in a trial with Cal Fire. At about 3 a.m. on 5 August 2023, the AI picked out a column of smoke in the Cleveland National Forest near Mount Laguna. That is about 40 miles east of San Diego. Human operators verified the detection. They alerted Cal Fire. On 24 August 2023 the Los Angeles Times reported that Scott Slumpff, a battalion chief at Cal Fire, got the confirmed alert just before 3 a.m. The Times reported that crews held the fire to a spot 10 feet by 10 feet. Slumpff said that without the alert nobody would have known about the fire until the next morning. He judged that it would probably have reached hundreds of acres. On 12 September 2023 AFP reported that the operators had alerted Cal Fire Captain Kris Yeary. It reported that his crews put the fire out at less than a quarter acre. Yeary told AFP that it could have become a devastating fire had the AI not alerted them. By September 2023 the tool reached all 21 Cal Fire dispatch centers. According to Cal Fire's figures for 2024, the cameras picked up 1,668 of 7,553 wildfires in its jurisdiction, 636 of them before any 911 call.

The area around Mount Laguna was spared a larger fire. Captain Yeary judged that it “could have been a devastating fire”. Battalion Chief Slumpff judged that it would probably have reached hundreds of acres. Neither judgment rests on a measurement of what would have happened without the alert.

data.retained_case_account: At about 3 am on 5 August 2023, the ALERTCalifornia AI flagged a column of smoke in the Cleveland National Forest near Mount Laguna. That is about 40 miles east of San Diego. The AI, a machine-learned model run by UC San Diego, watches live feeds from more than 1,000 cameras. Human operators verified the detection and alerted Cal Fire Captain Kris Yeary. His crews put it out at less than a quarter acre. Yeary told AFP that it could have become a devastating fire had the AI not alerted them. The AI watch over the feeds began at the end of June 2023 under a Cal Fire trial. By September 2023 the tool reached all 21 Cal Fire dispatch centers.

Human operators verified it before Cal Fire was alerted. The containment was done by Captain Yeary's crews. No source records whether a 911 call would have come later. The time gained is documented only for the program as a whole. TIME reports 77 fires identified before any 911 call in the first two months. UC San Diego's Neal Driscoll says the alerts beat 911 calls about 40 percent of the time. AFP also notes the system sometimes misreads dust, insects or weather as smoke. That is why the human verification step sits between the model and the dispatch.

fields.account: The ALERTCalifornia AI, a machine-learned model run by the University of California San Diego, scans live feeds from more than 1,000 cameras. It began scanning the feeds at the end of June 2023 in a trial with Cal Fire. At about 3 a.m. on 5 August 2023, the AI picked out a column of smoke in the Cleveland National Forest near Mount Laguna. That is about 40 miles east of San Diego. Human operators verified the detection. They alerted Cal Fire. On 24 August 2023 the Los Angeles Times reported that Scott Slumpff, a battalion chief at Cal Fire, got the confirmed alert just before 3 a.m. The Times reported that crews held the fire to a spot 10 feet by 10 feet. Slumpff said that without the alert nobody would have known about the fire until the next morning. He judged that it would probably have reached hundreds of acres. On 12 September 2023 AFP reported that the operators had alerted Cal Fire Captain Kris Yeary. It reported that his crews put the fire out at less than a quarter acre. Yeary told AFP that it could have become a devastating fire had the AI not alerted them. By September 2023 the tool reached all 21 Cal Fire dispatch centers. According to Cal Fire's figures for 2024, the cameras picked up 1,668 of 7,553 wildfires in its jurisdiction, 636 of them before any 911 call.

fields.summary: ALERTCalifornia's AI flagged smoke on a Cleveland National Forest camera at about 3 a.m. on 5 August 2023. Cal Fire held the verified fire under a quarter acre.
fields.account: The ALERTCalifornia AI, a machine-learned model run by the University of California San Diego, scans live feeds from more than 1,000 cameras. It began scanning the feeds at the end of June 2023 in a trial with Cal Fire. At about 3 a.m. on 5 August 2023, the AI picked out a column of smoke in the Cleveland National Forest near Mount Laguna. That is about 40 miles east of San Diego. Human operators verified the detection. They alerted Cal Fire. On 24 August 2023 the Los Angeles Times reported that Scott Slumpff, a battalion chief at Cal Fire, got the confirmed alert just before 3 a.m. The Times reported that crews held the fire to a spot 10 feet by 10 feet. Slumpff said that without the alert nobody would have known about the fire until the next morning. He judged that it would probably have reached hundreds of acres. On 12 September 2023 AFP reported that the operators had alerted Cal Fire Captain Kris Yeary. It reported that his crews put the fire out at less than a quarter acre. Yeary told AFP that it could have become a devastating fire had the AI not alerted them. By September 2023 the tool reached all 21 Cal Fire dispatch centers. According to Cal Fire's figures for 2024, the cameras picked up 1,668 of 7,553 wildfires in its jurisdiction, 636 of them before any 911 call.

record.title: Responders in Türkiye used machine-learning maps of damage from xView2 after the earthquakes of 6 February 2023
record.summary: xView2 is a machine-learning model that grades building damage in satellite images. After the 2023 Türkiye earthquakes, it gave responders maps that UN rescue teams used in Adıyaman.
record.account: In 2019 the Pentagon's Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) and Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute sponsored xView2, an open-source project to assess damage to buildings. The two bodies developed it. Partners included Microsoft and the University of California, Berkeley. It uses machine learning (semantic segmentation) on satellite imagery to identify damage to buildings. It grades the damage. The authors of Microsoft's February 2023 “Turkey Earthquake Report” include Microsoft AI for Good staff. Ritwik Gupta, DIU's principal AI scientist, is among them. They state that the team worked with Türkiye's Disaster and Emergency Management Presidency (AFAD) to deliver building-level damage estimates over four cities in southeast Türkiye. The report’s image dates range from 7 to 9 February 2023. The authors estimated 3,849 damaged buildings, including destroyed ones. Marash was the most affected, at 7.44% of buildings. MIT Technology Review reported on xView2 on 20 February 2023. Gupta told the magazine that at least two ground teams of search and rescue personnel from the UN's International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) had used xView2 in Adıyaman. Gupta said that it helped workers find damaged areas that they were unaware of. Gupta added that AFAD, the World Bank, the International Federation of the Red Cross (IFRC) and the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) had all used the platform. Atishay Abbhi, a World Bank disaster risk management specialist, said that the same degree of assessment would typically take weeks and now takes hours or minutes. The magazine gives 9 February 2023 as the first date with usable images. The technical report that it links includes 7 February imagery for Islahiye, with 9 February imagery for the other three cities. The magazine says that the model is up to 85 or 90% accurate. The World Bank does not mention xView2, AI or Microsoft in its GRADE report. No responder has described a decision taken on xView2 output. On 27 October 2025 researchers from Stanford University and Direct Relief published in PLOS Digital Health an outside test of the Microsoft model built on xBD, the dataset behind xView2. The test covered 38 facilities in three cities. Some were hospitals. The others were dialysis centers. The model found 42.86% of the damaged facilities. It correctly cleared 93.55% of the undamaged ones. The authors conclude that such models cannot yet replace ground surveys. In an article of 10 December 2025, Direct Relief describes this study of Microsoft and Google models. It does not describe a response decision.

data.retained_case_account: MIT Technology Review reported on 20 February 2023 on xView2, an open-source building-damage assessment project. It was sponsored and developed in 2019 by the Pentagon's Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) and Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute. Partners included Microsoft and UC Berkeley. It uses machine-learning (semantic segmentation) on satellite imagery to identify and grade building damage. Ritwik Gupta, DIU's principal AI scientist, told the magazine about use in Türkiye. At least two ground teams of search and rescue personnel from the UN's International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) had used xView2 in Adıyaman. He said it helped workers find damaged areas they were unaware of. He said AFAD, the World Bank, the IFRC and WFP had all used the platform. Atishay Abbhi, a World Bank disaster risk management specialist, said the same degree of assessment would typically take weeks and now takes hours or minutes. The article gives February 9, 2023, as the first usable-image date. However, the linked technical report includes February 7 imagery for Islahiye and February 9 imagery for the other three cities. It says the model is up to 85 or 90% accurate. Microsoft's February 2023 “Turkey Earthquake Report” has authors including Gupta and Microsoft AI for Good staff. It states that the team partnered with AFAD to deliver building-level damage estimates over four cities in southeast Türkiye. The report’s image dates range from February 7 to February 9. It estimated 3,849 buildings damaged or destroyed, with Marash the most affected at 7.44% of buildings. The World Bank GRADE report does not mention xView2, AI or Microsoft. DLR's peer-reviewed account states its own AI damage products were not part of the viewer delivered to responders. Direct Relief's December 2025 article describes a research study on Microsoft and Google models rather than a response decision. No responder statement describing a decision taken on xView2 output is among the sources.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The AI produced the damage classifications that responders are said to have used. Which decisions changed is not documented. Sources: the developer (DIU's Gupta) and the World Bank specialist, quoted in one news report, and Microsoft's own report of delivering estimates to AFAD. World Bank's GRADE report and DLR's account do not corroborate operational use of AI products.

fields.account: In 2019 the Pentagon's Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) and Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute sponsored xView2, an open-source project to assess damage to buildings. The two bodies developed it. Partners included Microsoft and the University of California, Berkeley. It uses machine learning (semantic segmentation) on satellite imagery to identify damage to buildings. It grades the damage. The authors of Microsoft's February 2023 “Turkey Earthquake Report” include Microsoft AI for Good staff. Ritwik Gupta, DIU's principal AI scientist, is among them. They state that the team worked with Türkiye's Disaster and Emergency Management Presidency (AFAD) to deliver building-level damage estimates over four cities in southeast Türkiye. The report’s image dates range from 7 to 9 February 2023. The authors estimated 3,849 damaged buildings, including destroyed ones. Marash was the most affected, at 7.44% of buildings. MIT Technology Review reported on xView2 on 20 February 2023. Gupta told the magazine that at least two ground teams of search and rescue personnel from the UN's International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) had used xView2 in Adıyaman. Gupta said that it helped workers find damaged areas that they were unaware of. Gupta added that AFAD, the World Bank, the International Federation of the Red Cross (IFRC) and the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) had all used the platform. Atishay Abbhi, a World Bank disaster risk management specialist, said that the same degree of assessment would typically take weeks and now takes hours or minutes. The magazine gives 9 February 2023 as the first date with usable images. The technical report that it links includes 7 February imagery for Islahiye, with 9 February imagery for the other three cities. The magazine says that the model is up to 85 or 90% accurate. The World Bank does not mention xView2, AI or Microsoft in its GRADE report. No responder has described a decision taken on xView2 output. On 27 October 2025 researchers from Stanford University and Direct Relief published in PLOS Digital Health an outside test of the Microsoft model built on xBD, the dataset behind xView2. The test covered 38 facilities in three cities. Some were hospitals. The others were dialysis centers. The model found 42.86% of the damaged facilities. fields.account: In 2019 the Pentagon's Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) and Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute sponsored xView2, an open-source project to assess damage to buildings. The two bodies developed it. Partners included Microsoft and the University of California, Berkeley. It uses machine learning (semantic segmentation) on satellite imagery to identify damage to buildings. It grades the damage. The authors of Microsoft's February 2023 “Turkey Earthquake Report” include Microsoft AI for Good staff. Ritwik Gupta, DIU's principal AI scientist, is among them. They state that the team worked with Türkiye's Disaster and Emergency Management Presidency (AFAD) to deliver building-level damage estimates over four cities in southeast Türkiye. The report’s image dates range from 7 to 9 February 2023. The authors estimated 3,849 damaged buildings, including destroyed ones. Marash was the most affected, at 7.44% of buildings. MIT Technology Review reported on xView2 on 20 February 2023. Gupta told the magazine that at least two ground teams of search and rescue personnel from the UN's International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) had used xView2 in Adıyaman. Gupta said that it helped workers find damaged areas that they were unaware of. Gupta added that AFAD, the World Bank, the International Federation of the Red Cross (IFRC) and the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) had all used the platform. Atishay Abbhi, a World Bank disaster risk management specialist, said that the same degree of assessment would typically take weeks and now takes hours or minutes. The magazine gives 9 February 2023 as the first date with usable images. The technical report that it links includes 7 February imagery for Islahiye, with 9 February imagery for the other three cities. The magazine says that the model is up to 85 or 90% accurate. The World Bank does not mention xView2, AI or Microsoft in its GRADE report. No responder has described a decision taken on xView2 output. On 27 October 2025 researchers from Stanford University and Direct Relief published in PLOS Digital Health an outside test of the Microsoft model built on xBD, the dataset behind xView2. The test covered 38 facilities in three cities. Some were hospitals. The others were dialysis centers. The model found 42.86% of the damaged facilities. It correctly cleared 93.55% of the undamaged ones. The authors conclude that such models cannot yet replace ground surveys. In an article of 10 December 2025, Direct Relief describes this study of Microsoft and Google models. It does not describe a response decision.

record.title: An alert about self-harm from Instagram to the cyber police of Madhya Pradesh leads Satna officers within about an hour to a 17-year-old who goes home after counseling (3 November 2022)
record.summary: An alert from Instagram's self-harm detection led Madhya Pradesh police to a 17-year-old in Satna within about an hour on 3 November 2022. She went home after counseling.
record.account: On 3 November 2022 at about 5 pm, Madhya Pradesh's state cyber police received an alert emailed by Instagram's US office. It said that a user in the state had suffered a body injury. The Indore cyber-crime unit shared the “self-harm” alert with the cyber headquarters in Bhopal (ANI, 5 November 2022, as well as Times of India, 4 November 2022). The girl, 17, had uploaded two videos. In one, a packet of poison lay beside her as she acted as if drunk. In the other she appeared to cut a vein (ANI). The Times of India notes a small cut on her wrist. Vaibhav Shrivastava, superintendent of police with the state cyber police, said: “After an effort of one hour, we traced the location of the girl”. She was in Satna district, whose police were informed (ANI). Ashutosh Gupta, the Satna superintendent of police, said that officers located her. He said that they called her in with her mother. She said that she only wanted to scare her boyfriend. She was sent home after counseling (Times of India). In January 2026 Decode reported that Meta reviews flagged posts before it alerts police. It reported that Meta publishes no data on false alarms. Decode also interviewed police in Uttar Pradesh. It described a false alarm in Kanpur Dehat. There a student said that she had posted a video with tablets only to gain views.

fields.summary: An alert from Instagram's self-harm detection led Madhya Pradesh police to a 17-year-old in Satna within about an hour on 3 November 2022. She went home after counseling.
fields.account: On 3 November 2022 at about 5 pm, Madhya Pradesh's state cyber police received an alert emailed by Instagram's US office. It said that a user in the state had suffered a body injury. The Indore cyber-crime unit shared the “self-harm” alert with the cyber headquarters in Bhopal (ANI, 5 November 2022, as well as Times of India, 4 November 2022). The girl, 17, had uploaded two videos. In one, a packet of poison lay beside her as she acted as if drunk. In the other she appeared to cut a vein (ANI). The Times of India notes a small cut on her wrist. Vaibhav Shrivastava, superintendent of police with the state cyber police, said: “After an effort of one hour, we traced the location of the girl”. She was in Satna district, whose police were informed (ANI). Ashutosh Gupta, the Satna superintendent of police, said that officers located her. He said that they called her in with her mother. She said that she only wanted to scare her boyfriend. She was sent home after counseling (Times of India). In January 2026 Decode reported that Meta reviews flagged posts before it alerts police. It reported that Meta publishes no data on false alarms. Decode also interviewed police in Uttar Pradesh. It described a false alarm in Kanpur Dehat. There a student said that she had posted a video with tablets only to gain views.

record.title: The Palantir-based DAR software identifies the author of an emailed amok threat against Siegen's city administration in fractions of a second. It identifies 51 of about 100 participants in a Duisburg shooting (28 October 2022)
record.summary: North Rhine-Westphalia's interior ministry says that its Palantir software traced an amok threat in Siegen in fractions of a second. The tool identified 51 of about 100 people at a Duisburg shooting.
record.account: In October 2022 someone emailed the city administration of Siegen announcing an amok attack. The threat was over the city's “topless” permission for swimming pools. A shooting in Duisburg-Hamborn between a Turkish-Arab clan and the Hells Angels injured four people. Interior Minister Herbert Reul addressed the Landtag's interior committee on 27 October. He said that DAR, the police's Palantir software, links the weapons register, residents' registration, the police case system and the wanted-persons portal. On 28 October 2022 the Interior Ministry of North Rhine-Westphalia said that DAR was central in several recent cases (WELT and RP Online). The ministry said that the email address revealed the suspect via Palantir in fractions of a second. A Duisburg investigator said that police quickly identified 51 of the roughly 100 participants in the shooting, at about 20 minutes each (RP Online and WELT). Of these, 49 were assigned to rival groups. The ministry puts the 2019–2025 cost at about 39 million euros. The opposition attacks the software on grounds of data protection, with its cost as a second ground (WELT). In October 2022 the civil-rights group Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte (GFF) filed a constitutional complaint against the state police law that allowed this data analysis. North Rhine-Westphalia rewrote the legal basis at the end of 2025. In February 2026 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to decide the complaint. It ordered the state to pay the complainants' costs (GFF).

fields.account: In October 2022 someone emailed the city administration of Siegen announcing an amok attack. The threat was over the city's “topless” permission for swimming pools. A shooting in Duisburg-Hamborn between a Turkish-Arab clan and the Hells Angels injured four people. Interior Minister Herbert Reul addressed the Landtag's interior committee on 27 October. He said that DAR, the police's Palantir software, links the weapons register, residents' registration, the police case system and the wanted-persons portal. On 28 October 2022 the Interior Ministry of North Rhine-Westphalia said that DAR was central in several recent cases (WELT and RP Online). The ministry said that the email address revealed the suspect via Palantir in fractions of a second. A Duisburg investigator said that police quickly identified 51 of the roughly 100 participants in the shooting, at about 20 minutes each (RP Online and WELT). Of these, 49 were assigned to rival groups. The ministry puts the 2019–2025 cost at about 39 million euros. The opposition attacks the software on grounds of data protection, with its cost as a second ground (WELT). In October 2022 the civil-rights group Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte (GFF) filed a constitutional complaint against the state police law that allowed this data analysis. North Rhine-Westphalia rewrote the legal basis at the end of 2025. In February 2026 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to decide the complaint. It ordered the state to pay the complainants' costs (GFF).

details.value: Google built the forecasting system to warn people of river floods before the water arrives, so that they can prepare or leave. The study measured what relaying those warnings did for groups of households.

details.label: Contribution of the AI
details.value: Both study arms received the same forecasts and alerts. record.title: Randomized evaluation of volunteers relaying AI-based flood warnings in Bihar, India (2022–2025 monsoons)
record.summary: In a trial in Bihar, volunteers relayed flood alerts from Google and the Central Water Commission. Under severe floods, their villages' homes were 12.7 percentage points less likely to flood.
record.account: Google's AI system for flood forecasting is run with India's Central Water Commission. It sends alerts of river floods as push notifications on Android. In Bihar, India, the economists Maulik Jagnani (Tufts) and Rohini Pande (Yale) ran a randomized evaluation across 319 panchayats (village councils) in 12 flood-prone districts. The non-governmental organization Yuganter trained community volunteers to relay the alerts in the treatment villages. Control villages received the same forecasts. They received the same alerts but had no volunteers. A working paper of 3 April 2024 covers the 2022 and 2023 monsoon seasons (June to October). The authors report that treatment households got 2.41 more alerts in 2022. They were 46.5% more likely to get an alert before water reached their area. In 2023 treatment households received 4.35 more alerts. They were 88% more likely to receive an alert before water reached their panchayat. Treatment households reported 16.56% fewer symptoms of illness than controls. They reported about 30% lower medical spending. The authors report that households in treatment areas spent roughly INR 6,500 less on treating illness, a 32.87% decrease. No specific evacuation tied to an alert is documented. A September 2026 version of the working paper covers four monsoon seasons from 2022 to 2025. The authors state that Google alerts were unavailable in 2022, when volunteers relayed Central Water Commission forecasts. From 2023 the volunteers relayed Google Flood Hub alerts along with Google's flood maps. The authors state that the experiment isolates the value of community delivery. They state that it does not measure the value of the forecasting systems. Among control households under severe flooding, the chance of home flooding was 23.7 percentage points higher than in a season with no flood. The authors report that treated households under severe flooding were 12.7 percentage points less likely to have their own home flooded. They borrowed about INR 12,600 less. They report that welfare gains concentrate in flooded villages, where the program raised a post-flood welfare index by 0.3 standard deviations. They report gains in food security. They report that the program had no effect on physical health. This version does not repeat the results of April 2024 on illness. It does not repeat those on medical spending. The authors acknowledge financial support from Google.org.

data.retained_case_account: Google's AI flood-forecasting system, run with India's Central Water Commission (CWC), issues riverine flood alerts as Android push notifications. In Bihar, India, economists Maulik Jagnani (Tufts) and Rohini Pande (Yale) ran a randomized evaluation across 319 panchayats in 12 flood-prone districts. It covered the 2022 and 2023 monsoon seasons (June to October). The non-governmental organization Yuganter trained community volunteers to relay the alerts. Treatment households got 2.41 more alerts in 2022 and were 46.5% more likely to get an alert before water reached their area. They reported 16.56% fewer illness symptoms and about 30% lower medical spending than controls. No specific evacuation tied to an alert is documented.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The AI forecast generated the alerts. The randomized contrast, however, is between community dissemination of those alerts and alerts alone. So the measured effect is attributable to the dissemination of AI forecasts rather than to forecast accuracy itself. A 2019 pilot in which the only added treatment was raising alert awareness with a single local leader found no treatment impact.

fields.account: Google's AI system for flood forecasting is run with India's Central Water Commission. It sends alerts of river floods as push notifications on Android. In Bihar, India, the economists Maulik Jagnani (Tufts) and Rohini Pande (Yale) ran a randomized evaluation across 319 panchayats (village councils) in 12 flood-prone districts. The non-governmental organization Yuganter trained community volunteers to relay the alerts in the treatment villages. Control villages received the same forecasts. They received the same alerts but had no volunteers. A working paper of 3 April 2024 covers the 2022 and 2023 monsoon seasons (June to October). The authors report that treatment households got 2.41 more alerts in 2022. They were 46.5% more likely to get an alert before water reached their area. In 2023 treatment households received 4.35 more alerts. They were 88% more likely to receive an alert before water reached their panchayat. Treatment households reported 16.56% fewer symptoms of illness than controls. They reported about 30% lower medical spending. The authors report that households in treatment areas spent roughly INR 6,500 less on treating illness, a 32.87% decrease. No specific evacuation tied to an alert is documented. A September 2026 version of the working paper covers four monsoon seasons from 2022 to 2025. The authors state that Google alerts were unavailable in 2022, when volunteers relayed Central Water Commission forecasts. From 2023 the volunteers relayed Google Flood Hub alerts along with Google's flood maps. The authors state that the experiment isolates the value of community delivery. They state that it does not measure the value of the forecasting systems. Among control households under severe flooding, the chance of home flooding was 23.7 percentage points higher than in a season with no flood. The authors report that treated households under severe flooding were 12.7 percentage points less likely to have their own home flooded. They borrowed about INR 12,600 less. They report that welfare gains concentrate in flooded villages, where the program raised a post-flood welfare index by 0.3 standard deviations. They report gains in food security. They report that the program had no effect on physical health. This version does not repeat the results of April 2024 on illness. It does not repeat those on medical spending. The authors acknowledge financial support from Google.org.

fields.summary: In a trial in Bihar, volunteers relayed flood alerts from Google and the Central Water Commission. Under severe floods, their villages' homes were 12.7 percentage points less likely to flood.
fields.account: Google's AI system for flood forecasting is run with India's Central Water Commission. It sends alerts of river floods as push notifications on Android. In Bihar, India, the economists Maulik Jagnani (Tufts) and Rohini Pande (Yale) ran a randomized evaluation across 319 panchayats (village councils) in 12 flood-prone districts. The non-governmental organization Yuganter trained community volunteers to relay the alerts in the treatment villages. Control villages received the same forecasts. They received the same alerts but had no volunteers. A working paper of 3 April 2024 covers the 2022 and 2023 monsoon seasons (June to October). The authors report that treatment households got 2.41 more alerts in 2022. They were 46.5% more likely to get an alert before water reached their area. In 2023 treatment households received 4.35 more alerts. They were 88% more likely to receive an alert before water reached their panchayat. Treatment households reported 16.56% fewer symptoms of illness than controls. They reported about 30% lower medical spending. The authors report that households in treatment areas spent roughly INR 6,500 less on treating illness, a 32.87% decrease. No specific evacuation tied to an alert is documented. A September 2026 version of the working paper covers four monsoon seasons from 2022 to 2025. The authors state that Google alerts were unavailable in 2022, when volunteers relayed Central Water Commission forecasts. From 2023 the volunteers relayed Google Flood Hub alerts along with Google's flood maps. The authors state that the experiment isolates the value of community delivery. They state that it does not measure the value of the forecasting systems. Among control households under severe flooding, the chance of home flooding was 23.7 percentage points higher than in a season with no flood. The authors report that treated households under severe flooding were 12.7 percentage points less likely to have their own home flooded. They borrowed about INR 12,600 less. They report that welfare gains concentrate in flooded villages, where the program raised a post-flood welfare index by 0.3 standard deviations. They report gains in food security. They report that the program had no effect on physical health. This version does not repeat the results of April 2024 on illness. It does not repeat those on medical spending. The authors acknowledge financial support from Google.org.

record.title: Westchester County police use Rekor's analysis of plate-reader patterns to stop a man in Scarsdale. Officers find crack cocaine. He is convicted
record.summary: Rekor Scout software flagged a man's trips past Westchester County's 480 plate-reader cameras. Officers who stopped him in Scarsdale on 10 March 2022 found crack cocaine. They found a pistol.
record.account: Carscoops reports that the Westchester County Police Department, New York, used technology provided by Rekor. It examined the driving patterns of anyone passing its 480 license-plate-reader cameras over a two-year period. It showed that a man had made several trips along routes typically used by drug traffickers. He had then turned around quickly to go home. According to The Star's AFP Relaxnews item, police took an interest in a vehicle registered to the man in March 2022. On 10 March 2022 the man was driving a gray Chevrolet in Scarsdale. Officers pulled him over. They searched the car. Carscoops reports that they found crack cocaine, cash and a pistol. Forbes reported that the search found 112 grams of crack cocaine, a semiautomatic pistol and $34,000 in cash. On 10 March 2023 the defense filed a motion to suppress the evidence from the location-data searches. The court never decided it. The federal docket shows that the man pleaded guilty on 28 June 2023. Forbes reported the story on 17 July 2023. Carscoops followed on 18 July 2023, drawing on Forbes. Carscoops quotes ACLU lawyer Brett Max Kaufman and defense attorney Ben Gold, who criticized the surveillance. On 24 January 2024 the man received 48 months, with a $34,000 forfeiture. A presidential commutation filed on 17 January 2025 ended his prison term on 16 May 2025. The conviction stands, with three years of supervised release.

fields.account: Carscoops reports that the Westchester County Police Department, New York, used technology provided by Rekor. It examined the driving patterns of anyone passing its 480 license-plate-reader cameras over a two-year period. It showed that a man had made several trips along routes typically used by drug traffickers. He had then turned around quickly to go home. According to The Star's AFP Relaxnews item, police took an interest in a vehicle registered to the man in March 2022. On 10 March 2022 the man was driving a gray Chevrolet in Scarsdale. Officers pulled him over. They searched the car. Carscoops reports that they found crack cocaine, cash and a pistol. Forbes reported that the search found 112 grams of crack cocaine, a semiautomatic pistol and $34,000 in cash. On 10 March 2023 the defense filed a motion to suppress the evidence from the location-data searches. The court never decided it. The federal docket shows that the man pleaded guilty on 28 June 2023. Forbes reported the story on 17 July 2023. Carscoops followed on 18 July 2023, drawing on Forbes. Carscoops quotes ACLU lawyer Brett Max Kaufman and defense attorney Ben Gold, who criticized the surveillance. On 24 January 2024 the man received 48 months, with a $34,000 forfeiture. A presidential commutation filed on 17 January 2025 ended his prison term on 16 May 2025. The conviction stands, with three years of supervised release.

details.value: Boulder Imaging built IdentiFlight to detect and classify flying eagles and to curtail individual turbines, so that eagles do not collide with them.

details.label: Contribution of the AI
details.value: The system's classifications trigger curtailment, so any fall in deaths runs through the AI. The authors of the peer-reviewed estimate have no tie to the maker, but two statisticians challenged it in a peer-reviewed reanalysis (50%, with an interval that includes zero). In the California assessment, the system missed 23% of eagles and issued six times more virtual orders for other birds than for eagles. Those orders did not slow the California turbines. So the size of the benefit is unsettled.

record.title: IdentiFlight stops wind turbines when it detects eagles at a Wyoming wind farm, where disputed estimates put the cut in eagle deaths at 50% to 82%
record.summary: Researchers estimated an 82% (75%–89%) relative cut in eagle deaths at a Wyoming wind farm after IdentiFlight began curtailing turbines. Two federal statisticians later put it at 50% (−159%, 89%).
record.account: McClure et al. tested an automated curtailment system at the Top of the World Windpower Facility in Wyoming, United States. The authors are from The Peregrine Fund, Western EcoSystems Technology and the U.S. Geological Survey. The system's cameras detect flying objects. They classify them. The system curtails individual turbines. The design was before–after–control–impact, with a control site 15 km away. Recharge reported the claim on 28 January 2021. The study appeared in the Journal of Applied Ecology (Crossref publication date 31 January 2021). Correcting for carcass detection probability, the authors estimated that fatalities fell 63% at the treatment site (95% confidence interval 59%–66%). Fatalities rose 113% at the control site. Relative to the control site, this is an 82% (75%–89%) reduction. The authors noted that fatalities were not eliminated. On 26 August 2022 the same authors reported more data from the same site in Ecological Solutions and Evidence. With it, eagle fatalities fell by 85% (95% highest density interval 12% to 100%). Duerr et al. (PLoS One, 26 January 2023) assessed an IdentiFlight installation in California. It classified 77% of eagles correctly. It classified 85% of other targets correctly. It issued 5,439 virtual curtailment orders for non-eagle targets against 850 for eagles. These orders did not slow the turbines. Huso and Dalthorp (Journal of Applied Ecology, 30 August 2023) reanalyzed the Wyoming data and reported four major errors. They reported that the corrected data give 50% (−159%, 89%), consistent with no effect. McClure et al. replied the same day that their data support the efficacy of automated curtailment. In its final eagle permit rule of 12 February 2024, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service answered comments that asked for IdentiFlight in permit conditions. The Service said that permittees may use such technologies but that their efficacy has not been studied enough to require them.

ratings.reason: McClure et al. report that eagle fatalities at the treatment site fell by 63% after automated curtailment, a measurable improvement in a conservation result. Two U.S. Geological Survey statisticians reanalyzed the data and put the effect at 50%, with an interval that includes an increase, so the size of the effect is disputed.

data.retained_case_account: McClure et al. (Journal of Applied Ecology, Crossref publication date 31 January 2021) tested an automated curtailment system. The site was Top of the World Windpower Facility, Wyoming, USA. Authors are from The Peregrine Fund, Western EcoSystems Technology and the U.S. Geological Survey. The cameras detect and classify flying objects and decide whether to curtail individual turbines. The design was before–after–control–impact, with a control site 15 km away. Correcting for carcass detection probability, they estimated fatalities fell 63% at the treatment site (95% confidence interval, CI, 59%–66%). They rose 113% at the control site, an 82% (75%–89%) relative reduction. They noted fatalities were not eliminated. Recharge reported the claim on 28 January 2021. Huso and Dalthorp (Journal of Applied Ecology, 30 August 2023) reanalyzed the data and reported four major errors. Corrected, these give 50% (−159%, 89%), consistent with no effect. McClure et al. replied the same day that their data support the efficacy of automated curtailment. Duerr et al. (PLoS One, 26 January 2023) assessed an IdentiFlight installation in California. It correctly identified 77% of eagles and 85% of non-eagles, with 5,439 virtual curtailment orders for non-eagle targets against 850 for eagles. These orders did not slow the turbines.

fields.account: McClure et al. tested an automated curtailment system at the Top of the World Windpower Facility in Wyoming, United States. The authors are from The Peregrine Fund, Western EcoSystems Technology and the U.S. Geological Survey. The system's cameras detect flying objects. They classify them. The system curtails individual turbines. The design was before–after–control–impact, with a control site 15 km away. Recharge reported the claim on 28 January 2021. The study appeared in the Journal of Applied Ecology (Crossref publication date 31 January 2021). Correcting for carcass detection probability, the authors estimated that fatalities fell 63% at the treatment site (95% confidence interval 59%–66%). Fatalities rose 113% at the control site. Relative to the control site, this is an 82% (75%–89%) reduction. The authors noted that fatalities were not eliminated. On 26 August 2022 the same authors reported more data from the same site in Ecological Solutions and Evidence. With it, eagle fatalities fell by 85% (95% highest density interval 12% to 100%). Duerr et al. (PLoS One, 26 January 2023) assessed an IdentiFlight installation in California. It classified 77% of eagles correctly. It classified 85% of other targets correctly. It issued 5,439 virtual curtailment orders for non-eagle targets against 850 for eagles. These orders did not slow the turbines. Huso and Dalthorp (Journal of Applied Ecology, 30 August 2023) reanalyzed the Wyoming data and reported four major errors. They reported that the corrected data give 50% (−159%, 89%), consistent with no effect. McClure et al. replied the same day that their data support the efficacy of automated curtailment. In its final eagle permit rule of 12 February 2024, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service answered comments that asked for IdentiFlight in permit conditions. The Service said that permittees may use such technologies but that their efficacy has not been studied enough to require them.

display.answer: The Wyoming estimates all draw on data from one site. They come from the 2021 study by McClure et al., their 2022 confirmation, the 2023 reanalysis by Huso and Dalthorp and the authors' reply. The California study by Duerr et al. Measured a separate installation.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: Researchers estimated an 82% (75%–89%) relative cut in eagle deaths at a Wyoming wind farm after IdentiFlight began curtailing turbines. Two federal statisticians later put it at 50% (−159%, 89%).
fields.account: McClure et al. tested an automated curtailment system at the Top of the World Windpower Facility in Wyoming, United States. The authors are from The Peregrine Fund, Western EcoSystems Technology and the U.S. Geological Survey. The system's cameras detect flying objects. They classify them. The system curtails individual turbines. The design was before–after–control–impact, with a control site 15 km away. Recharge reported the claim on 28 January 2021. The study appeared in the Journal of Applied Ecology (Crossref publication date 31 January 2021). Correcting for carcass detection probability, the authors estimated that fatalities fell 63% at the treatment site (95% confidence interval 59%–66%). Fatalities rose 113% at the control site. Relative to the control site, this is an 82% (75%–89%) reduction. The authors noted that fatalities were not eliminated. On 26 August 2022 the same authors reported more data from the same site in Ecological Solutions and Evidence. With it, eagle fatalities fell by 85% (95% highest density interval 12% to 100%). Duerr et al. (PLoS One, 26 January 2023) assessed an IdentiFlight installation in California. It classified 77% of eagles correctly. It classified 85% of other targets correctly. It issued 5,439 virtual curtailment orders for non-eagle targets against 850 for eagles. These orders did not slow the turbines. Huso and Dalthorp (Journal of Applied Ecology, 30 August 2023) reanalyzed the Wyoming data and reported four major errors. They reported that the corrected data give 50% (−159%, 89%), consistent with no effect. McClure et al. replied the same day that their data support the efficacy of automated curtailment. In its final eagle permit rule of 12 February 2024, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service answered comments that asked for IdentiFlight in permit conditions. The Service said that permittees may use such technologies but that their efficacy has not been studied enough to require them.

record.title: In a one-week pilot in 2017, VeriPol flags 25 false robbery reports in Murcia. It flags 39 in Málaga. Spain's police drop it in 2024
record.summary: In a pilot week in June 2017, the Spanish National Police's VeriPol text classifier flagged 25 false robbery reports in Murcia. It flagged 39 in Málaga. The police stopped using it on 21 October 2024.
record.account: VeriPol, a model for detecting false robbery reports from their text, was developed by researchers at the Complutense and Carlos III universities with police officer Miguel Camacho-Collados. A pilot study in Murcia and Málaga ran for one week in June 2017. The model appeared in Knowledge-Based Systems (Quijano-Sánchez, Liberatore, Camacho-Collados and Camacho-Collados, 2018). In the abstract, the authors report a validation accuracy of 91% on more than 1,000 reports from 2015, an improvement of more than 15% over expert officers. They report that the pilot study showed a lower bound on empirical precision of about 83%. Civio reported that the Interior Ministry announced nationwide use in 2018. On 1 February 2019 Scientific American reported on the pilot week in Murcia and Málaga. Police in the pilot detected 25 and 39 false robberies respectively, against 3 and 12 in the same month over the previous decade. It quoted Camacho Collados on colleagues wasting time on crimes that never occurred. According to Civio, the police analyzed 49,702 complaints in 2019 and deemed 2,338 of them false. AlgorithmWatch (27 October 2020) found no independent verification of effectiveness since deployment. Civio reported that in 2022 the police analyzed 3,762 complaints and deemed 511 of them false. In a report for the University of Valencia in September 2024, Lucía Martínez Garay and colleagues criticized the training sample of 1,122 reports. They objected to the lack of training for officers. They faulted the lack of regional variation in language. They found that the authors of the 2017 pilot paper gave neither case counts nor a confusion matrix. The police told them that VeriPol still needed an evaluation of its performance that had not been possible to carry out. The Interior Ministry told Civio that the police stopped using VeriPol on 21 October 2024. Civio (25 March 2025) reported that the Ministry said that the police stopped because the tool was not valid in judicial proceedings. According to Civio, the VeriPol team's academic article says that in 83.54% of reports marked false the complainant confessed.

data.retained_case_account: VeriPol, a model for detecting false robbery reports from their text, was developed by Complutense and Carlos III university researchers with police officer Miguel Camacho-Collados. It appeared in Knowledge-Based Systems (Quijano-Sánchez, Liberatore, Camacho-Collados and Camacho-Collados, 2018). The abstract reports a validation accuracy of 91% on more than 1,000 reports from 2015, an improvement of more than 15% over expert officers. It reports a pilot study in June 2017 showing a lower bound on empirical precision of about 83%. Scientific American (1 February 2019) reported that the one-week pilot in Murcia and Málaga detected 25 and 39 false robberies respectively. The same month over the previous decade had 3 and 12. It quoted Camacho Collados on colleagues wasting time on cases that never occurred. Civio (25 March 2025) reported that the police said that in 83.54% of reports flagged false the complainant confessed. It also reported the Interior Ministry's 2018 announcement of nationwide use. Complaints analyzed were 49,702 in 2019 with 2,338 deemed false, and 3,762 in 2022 with 511 deemed false. Use stopped on 21 October 2024 because the tool was not valid in judicial proceedings, it said. A University of Valencia report (September 2024) criticized the 1,122-report training sample, missing officer training and regional language variation. AlgorithmWatch (27 October 2020) found no independent verification of effectiveness since deployment. The pilot month carries no day.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The peer-reviewed paper describes a natural-language-processing and machine-learning classifier with L1 feature selection that outputs the probability a report is false. The paper's authors include the police developer. AlgorithmWatch and Civio report that no independent verification was done before the police stopped using it in October 2024.

fields.account: VeriPol, a model for detecting false robbery reports from their text, was developed by researchers at the Complutense and Carlos III universities with police officer Miguel Camacho-Collados. A pilot study in Murcia and Málaga ran for one week in June 2017. The model appeared in Knowledge-Based Systems (Quijano-Sánchez, Liberatore, Camacho-Collados and Camacho-Collados, 2018). In the abstract, the authors report a validation accuracy of 91% on more than 1,000 reports from 2015, an improvement of more than 15% over expert officers. They report that the pilot study showed a lower bound on empirical precision of about 83%. Civio reported that the Interior Ministry announced nationwide use in 2018. On 1 February 2019 Scientific American reported on the pilot week in Murcia and Málaga. Police in the pilot detected 25 and 39 false robberies respectively, against 3 and 12 in the same month over the previous decade. It quoted Camacho Collados on colleagues wasting time on crimes that never occurred. According to Civio, the police analyzed 49,702 complaints in 2019 and deemed 2,338 of them false. AlgorithmWatch (27 October 2020) found no independent verification of effectiveness since deployment. Civio reported that in 2022 the police analyzed 3,762 complaints and deemed 511 of them false. In a report for the University of Valencia in September 2024, Lucía Martínez Garay and colleagues criticized the training sample of 1,122 reports. They objected to the lack of training for officers. They faulted the lack of regional variation in language. They found that the authors of the 2017 pilot paper gave neither case counts nor a confusion matrix. The police told them that VeriPol still needed an evaluation of its performance that had not been possible to carry out. The Interior Ministry told Civio that the police stopped using VeriPol on 21 October 2024. Civio (25 March 2025) reported that the Ministry said that the police stopped because the tool was not valid in judicial proceedings. According to Civio, the VeriPol team's academic article says that in 83.54% of reports marked false the complainant confessed.

record.summary: Bank F's unnamed tool for network analytics linked a third company to a suspected money laundering network through shared phone numbers.
record.account: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority's report “AML/CFT Regtech: Case Studies and Insights” presents anonymized case studies of banks. It appeared in January 2021, with a press release on 21 January 2021. The authors describe Bank F as a subsidiary and regional head office of a large global bank in Asia-Pacific. They state that before the tool, manual reviews of documentation for signatories were the only means to make such connections. Bank F implemented a network (graph) analytics solution in Hong Kong in 2013. The solution identifies high-risk customers from the data. It identifies high-risk transactions. The data cover wholesale clients. They cover correspondent banking. They cover trade. They cover payments. They cover external registries. In an example from 2015, a relationship manager gathered intelligence about trade-based money laundering related to a drug cartel in one account. The manager linked it to a second account through the customer relationship management tool. The network tool then found more companies linked to the first two parties through shared phone numbers. It used shared email addresses. Reviews of the accounts of Companies A, B and C revealed potential money laundering concerns. The authors give no day for the example of 2015. They state that by 2016 Bank F covered its top 20 commercial banking sites and about 80% of its trade lending book. They say that the tool has led to the review of around 100 customer relationships holding around USD 500 million in clean or unsecured exposures. For their figure of USD 50 million, they assume that 10% of those exposures would otherwise be unrecoverable. They document no realized savings of USD 50 million. They add that by January 2021 a successor tool, built with an outside vendor, was in production in several jurisdictions. It drew on a data lake of over 40 billion rows. In the foreword, the authority adds that such techniques are already neutralizing networks of mule accounts linked to face mask scams.

They state that before the tool, manual reviews of documentation for signatories were the only means to make such connections. Bank F implemented a network (graph) analytics solution in Hong Kong in 2013. The solution identifies high-risk customers from the data. It identifies high-risk transactions. The data cover wholesale clients. They cover correspondent banking. They cover trade. They cover payments. They cover external registries. In an example from 2015, a relationship manager gathered intelligence about trade-based money laundering related to a drug cartel in one account. The manager linked it to a second account through the customer relationship management tool. The network tool then found more companies linked to the first two parties through shared phone numbers. It used shared email addresses. Reviews of the accounts of Companies A, B and C revealed potential money laundering concerns. The authors give no day for the example of 2015. They state that by 2016 Bank F covered its top 20 commercial banking sites and about 80% of its trade lending book. They say that the tool has led to the review of around 100 customer relationships holding around USD 500 million in clean or unsecured exposures. For their figure of USD 50 million, they assume that 10% of those exposures would otherwise be unrecoverable. They document no realized savings of USD 50 million. They add that by January 2021 a successor tool, built with an outside vendor, was in production in several jurisdictions. It drew on a data lake of over 40 billion rows. In the foreword, the authority adds that such techniques are already neutralizing networks of mule accounts linked to face mask scams.

record.title: Global Fishing Watch data lets Kiribati fine a vessel US$1 million for fishing in the Phoenix Islands Protected Area
record.summary: Kiribati used Global Fishing Watch to document a vessel fishing illegally in the Phoenix Islands Protected Area. The owner faced a US$1 million fine plus a US$1 million goodwill grant.
record.account: Global Fishing Watch was developed by Oceana, SkyTruth and Google. It processes automatic identification system tracks of tens of thousands of vessels. In Oceana's description, it uses machine learning to identify when they are fishing. It uses cloud computing for the work. Kiribati closed the Phoenix Islands Protected Area to commercial fishing on 1 January 2015. Oceana's Jacqueline Savitz wrote in 2018 that Global Fishing Watch revealed illegal fishing in the area a few months after the closure. The platform launched publicly at the Our Ocean conference on 15 September 2016. The Washington Post reported that before the launch the government of Kiribati had used it to document how a tuna-fishing vessel had operated illegally inside the protected area. That resulted in a US$1 million fine. Oceana board member Ted Danson wrote in Grist that the vessel was the Marshall Islands-flagged Marshalls 203. The fine was against its owner, Central Pacific Fishing Company. A goodwill arrangement to pay a further US$1 million as a grant came with it. The cited sources do not date the fine. In June 2017 Indonesia became the first country to publish its vessel monitoring system data through Global Fishing Watch. Savitz wrote in BBC Future in 2018 that the technology helped Kiribati extract a US$2 million fine, about 1% of gross domestic product. A 2018 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, by economists funded in part by Google, used Global Fishing Watch data. The economists found that fishing in the protected area had more than doubled before the closure. They found that it fell to nearly zero after it.

fields.summary: Kiribati used Global Fishing Watch to document a vessel fishing illegally in the Phoenix Islands Protected Area. The owner faced a US$1 million fine plus a US$1 million goodwill grant.
fields.account: Global Fishing Watch was developed by Oceana, SkyTruth and Google. It processes automatic identification system tracks of tens of thousands of vessels. In Oceana's description, it uses machine learning to identify when they are fishing. It uses cloud computing for the work. Kiribati closed the Phoenix Islands Protected Area to commercial fishing on 1 January 2015. Oceana's Jacqueline Savitz wrote in 2018 that Global Fishing Watch revealed illegal fishing in the area a few months after the closure. The platform launched publicly at the Our Ocean conference on 15 September 2016. The Washington Post reported that before the launch the government of Kiribati had used it to document how a tuna-fishing vessel had operated illegally inside the protected area. That resulted in a US$1 million fine. Oceana board member Ted Danson wrote in Grist that the vessel was the Marshall Islands-flagged Marshalls 203. The fine was against its owner, Central Pacific Fishing Company. A goodwill arrangement to pay a further US$1 million as a grant came with it. The cited sources do not date the fine. In June 2017 Indonesia became the first country to publish its vessel monitoring system data through Global Fishing Watch. Savitz wrote in BBC Future in 2018 that the technology helped Kiribati extract a US$2 million fine, about 1% of gross domestic product. A 2018 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, by economists funded in part by Google, used Global Fishing Watch data. The economists found that fishing in the protected area had more than doubled before the closure. They found that it fell to nearly zero after it.

record.title: NCAR's DICast cuts the error of Xcel Energy's wind forecasts to 10.8%, with savings that Xcel estimates at US$49 million
record.summary: NCAR's adaptive system for blending forecasts (DICast), used by Xcel Energy since 2009, cut mean wind forecast error from about 18% to 10.8% by 2014. Xcel estimated that it saved US$49m.
record.account: NCAR's wind power forecasting system for Xcel Energy blends numerical weather models with the Dynamic Integrated foreCast (DICast) system. DICast constantly checks its predictions against outcomes. It adjusts its bias corrections. It adjusts its weightings. The Xcel, NREL and UCAR authors of a 2011 NREL report state that the NCAR system entered Xcel's operations between November 2009 and April 2010. They found that day-ahead error at Public Service Company of Colorado fell from 18% in 2009 to 14.3% in 2010. A UCAR news item (7 February 2012) said that the system saved ratepayers $6 million in 2010 alone. It described the work as building on NCAR research ranging from statistics to artificial intelligence. On 23 April 2014 MIT Technology Review described the software as based on artificial intelligence. It reported that the forecasts saved Xcel nearly as much money in 2013 as in the three previous years combined. Sue Ellen Haupt and William Mahoney of the National Center for Atmospheric Research wrote in IEEE Spectrum (22 October 2015) that DICast had been used for wind prediction since 2009. The mean forecast error at a typical wind farm fell from about 18 percent in 2008 to 10.8 percent by 2014. Xcel estimated that the improvements had saved customers US$49 million so far. E&E News (4 December 2017) quoted Haupt as saying that the forecasts could save $10 million a year. It reported that Xcel operators decommit large coal units when sustained wind is predicted. None of the sources describes the system as machine learning in so many words. The savings are Xcel's estimates, reported through NCAR and the press. No regulator has audited them.

data.answer:
NCAR's adaptive forecast-blending system (DICast), used by Xcel Energy since 2009, cut mean wind forecast error from about 18% to 10.8% by 2014; Xcel estimated US$49m saved (IEEE Spectrum 2015).

Forecast error improved, while Xcel's cumulative US$49 million saving remains an attributed estimate. The adaptive weighting description does not establish exactly which learned technique generated the gain. The later US$10 million annual estimate is not an independent verification of the cumulative total.

The forecasting system's contribution to savings is Xcel's own estimate relayed by NCAR authors and reporters. The AI character of the system rests on UCAR's reference to artificial-intelligence research and DICast's adaptive bias correction, not on an explicit machine-learning description. So both the AI status and the causal share are unverified.

data.retained_case_account: Sue Ellen Haupt and William Mahoney of the National Center for Atmospheric Research wrote in IEEE Spectrum (22 October 2015). NCAR's wind power forecasting system for Xcel Energy blends numerical weather models with the Dynamic Integrated foreCast (DICast) system, used for wind prediction since 2009. DICast constantly checks its predictions against outcomes and adjusts its bias corrections and weightings. The mean forecast error at a typical wind farm fell from about 18 percent in 2008 to 10.8 percent by 2014. Xcel estimated the improvements had saved customers US$49 million so far. A UCAR news item (7 February 2012) said the system saved ratepayers $6 million in 2010 alone. It described the work as building on NCAR research ranging from statistics to artificial intelligence. E&E News (4 December 2017) quoted Haupt that the forecasts could save $10 million a year. It reported that Xcel operators decommit large coal units when sustained wind is predicted. None of the sources describes the system as machine learning in so many words. The savings are Xcel's estimates reported through NCAR and the press, not a regulator's audit.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The forecasting system's contribution to savings is Xcel's own estimate relayed by NCAR authors and reporters. The AI character of the system rests on UCAR's reference to artificial-intelligence research and DICast's adaptive bias correction, not on an explicit machine-learning description. So both the AI status and the causal share are unverified.

details.value: In its consumer terms (effective 8 October 2025), Anthropic reserves the right “at our sole discretion” to report Inputs to law enforcement. Its privacy policy (effective 10 September 2026) allows disclosure that the company believes “reasonably necessary” to “prevent serious harm to any person or to property”. In the arrest report, the platform's safety measures are described as “designed to monitor for key phrases and potentially threatening content”. Of a referral in August 2026, Anthropic said: “This is our safeguards process working as intended”.

details.label: Contribution of the AI
details.value: In the arrest report, the detective writes that the platform “utilizes safety and security measures designed to monitor for key phrases and potentially threatening content”. The detective writes that the messages were “escalated to a human review team”. So an automated layer surfaced the two messages, and people judged their severity and made the referral. Anthropic has not said whether the flag came from a classifier or a keyword rule. Straight Arrow News, citing court records, says that the review team escalated to the FBI, which notified the sheriff's office. Lee County deputies and Intelligence Detective Thomas Alejo identified the user, visited her home, interviewed her under Miranda and decided on the charge. In the arrest report, the platform is called “Anthropic Artificial Intelligence”. Reporters name Claude, and according to court records the user told the detective that she used Perplexity.

record.title: After Anthropic's threat monitoring flags a Bonita Springs woman's messages about shooting up the Lee County Sheriff's Office, human reviewers tip police, who detain her without incident
record.summary: Anthropic's safety monitoring flagged a chat user's threat to shoot up a Florida sheriff's office. After human review, the tip led deputies to detain her. No weapon was seized.
record.account: A user of Anthropic's AI chat service wrote at about 05:10 on 26 September 2026. She said that she was going to “shoot up” the Lee County Sheriff's Office in Florida. At 01:07 on 27 September she wrote that she had got a new gun. Anthropic's safety monitoring picked out the messages. Because of their severity a human review team reported them to law enforcement. Straight Arrow News, citing court records, reported that the review team escalated to the FBI, which notified the sheriff's office. The sheriff's office logged the tip on 29 September. It identified the user as a 30-year-old woman from Bonita Springs. Deputies detained her at home without incident at 00:51 on 30 September. A detective charged her under Florida Statute 836.10, written threats of violence. No weapon was seized. She described the AI as a personal diary. In the arrest report, the platform is called “Anthropic Artificial Intelligence”. Press reports name Claude. Court records note that the user told the detective that she used Perplexity. The arrest form set a $10,000 bond and a 20 October 2026 appearance date. The woman pleaded not guilty. Her arraignment was set for 2 November 2026, while prosecutors had not yet filed a formal charge. The First Amendment scholar Eugene Volokh doubts that the charge will hold.

display.answer: The platform's monitoring flagged the two messages automatically, and a human review team judged their severity and referred them to law enforcement. The sources leave open whether a classifier or a keyword rule raised the flag. ai_role.statement: In the arrest report, the detective writes that the platform “utilizes safety and security measures designed to monitor for key phrases and potentially threatening content”. The detective writes that the messages were “escalated to a human review team”. So an automated layer surfaced the two messages, and people judged their severity and made the referral. Anthropic has not said whether the flag came from a classifier or a keyword rule. Straight Arrow News, citing court records, says that the review team escalated to the FBI, which notified the sheriff's office. Lee County deputies and Intelligence Detective Thomas Alejo identified the user, visited her home, interviewed her under Miranda and decided on the charge. In the arrest report, the platform is called “Anthropic Artificial Intelligence”. Reporters name Claude, and according to court records the user told the detective that she used Perplexity.

data.retained_case_account: A user of Anthropic's AI chat service wrote at about 05:10 on 26 September 2026. She said she was going to “shoot up” the Lee County Sheriff's Office in Florida. At 01:07 on 27 September she wrote that she had got a new gun. Anthropic's safety monitoring flagged the messages, and because of their severity a human review team reported them to law enforcement. The sheriff's office logged the tip on 29 September and identified the user as a 30-year-old woman from Bonita Springs. Deputies detained her at home without incident at 00:51 on 30 September. A detective charged her under Florida Statute 836.10, written threats of violence. No weapon was seized, and she described the AI as a personal diary.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The arrest report says the platform “utilizes safety and security measures designed to monitor for key phrases and potentially threatening content”. It says the messages were “escalated to a human review team”. An automated layer therefore surfaced the two messages, and people judged their severity and made the referral. The sources do not say whether the flag came from a classifier or a keyword rule. Straight Arrow News, citing court records, says the review team escalated to the FBI, which notified the sheriff's office. Identifying the user, the home visit, the Miranda interview and the charging decision were the work of Lee County deputies and Intelligence Detective Thomas Alejo. The arrest report calls the platform “Anthropic Artificial Intelligence”. Press reports name Claude, and court records note the user told the detective she used Perplexity.

fields.summary: Anthropic's safety monitoring flagged a chat user's threat to shoot up a Florida sheriff's office. After human review, the tip led deputies to detain her. No weapon was seized.
fields.account: A user of Anthropic's AI chat service wrote at about 05:10 on 26 September 2026. She said that she was going to “shoot up” the Lee County Sheriff's Office in Florida. At 01:07 on 27 September she wrote that she had got a new gun. Anthropic's safety monitoring picked out the messages. Because of their severity a human review team reported them to law enforcement. Straight Arrow News, citing court records, reported that the review team escalated to the FBI, which notified the sheriff's office. The sheriff's office logged the tip on 29 September. It identified the user as a 30-year-old woman from Bonita Springs. Deputies detained her at home without incident at 00:51 on 30 September. A detective charged her under Florida Statute 836.10, written threats of violence. No weapon was seized. She described the AI as a personal diary. In the arrest report, the platform is called “Anthropic Artificial Intelligence”. Press reports name Claude. Court records note that the user told the detective that she used Perplexity. The arrest form set a $10,000 bond and a 20 October 2026 appearance date. The woman pleaded not guilty. Her arraignment was set for 2 November 2026, while prosecutors had not yet filed a formal charge. The First Amendment scholar Eugene Volokh doubts that the charge will hold.
